title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
NoteWork in progress



This optional track adds engineering mathematics and modelling to regular Computer Engineering Technology work. It is locally developed, is not endorsed by a college or university, and does not guarantee admission or postsecondary credit. Some assignments and the thermal-process project still require classroom testing.
Use this page as a pathway map. The TEJ sidebar contains the available lessons, worksheets, labs, projects, and reference notes. Detailed implementation planning belongs in the teacher guide.
The chapter names use terminology found in current University of Waterloo engineering programs, including Chemical Engineering and Mechatronics Engineering.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Full progression

0. Engineering design and communication
1. Units, engineering notation, and estimation
2. Ohm’s law and electrical power
3. Series, parallel, and series-parallel circuits
4. Kirchhoff’s laws and systems of equations
5. Equivalent circuits and optimization
6. Material and energy balances
7. Resistor-capacitor and thermal transients
8. Sensors, measurement, calibration, and uncertainty
9. Curve fitting, regression, and machine learning
10. Motors and electromechanical systems
11. Boolean logic, algorithms, and state machines
12. Sensor, logic, and actuator project
13. Number systems and digital representation
14. Feedback and control systems
15. Engineering design project

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
0. Engineering design and communication
Learning goal: Use an engineering notebook to record requirements, assumptions, diagrams, equations, units, test results, and revisions.
Why it matters: Clear records make work easier to check, improve, and explain.
Subsections:

Engineering baseline
Engineering notebook
Assumptions and evidence
Technical communication

Coming out of this chapter, students can: document a technical problem and show a complete, checkable solution process.
Suggested work: Engineering baseline diagnostic, correction record, learning targets, and notebook setup.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
1. Units, engineering notation, and estimation
Learning goal: Convert International System of Units quantities and metric prefixes; use engineering notation, significant figures, dimensional analysis, ratios, rates, and estimation.
Why it matters: Good units and estimates help catch calculator mistakes.
Subsections:

Units and dimensions
Engineering notation
Significant figures
Ratios and rates
Estimation

Coming out of this chapter, students can: convert, estimate, calculate, and communicate technical quantities reliably.
Related TEJ resources: Number Systems, Measurement, Units, and Calculator Skills
Suggested work: Assignment 1: quantity and unit audit.
References: [1, Ch. 0] [27, Ch. 1] [28, Chs. 1, 3]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
2. Ohm’s law and electrical power
Learning goal: Calculate voltage, current, resistance, and power using Ohm’s law and the power equations; rearrange equations and check component limits.
Why it matters: These calculations predict whether a circuit will work safely.
Subsections:

Charge
Voltage
Current
Resistance
Ohm’s law
Electrical power
Operating limits

Coming out of this chapter, students can: derive and check a resistive design rather than only substitute into a formula.
Related TEJ resources: Basic Electronics
Suggested work: Complete the Basic Circuit Calculations worksheet, then prepare Assignment 2: resistive design brief.
Reference: [1, Chs. 1, 3]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
3. Series, parallel, and series-parallel circuits
Learning goal: Calculate equivalent resistance, source current, branch current, voltage drops, and power in series, parallel, and series-parallel resistor circuits.
Why it matters: Students can predict circuit behaviour before building and find faults afterward.
Subsections:

Series resistance and voltage drops
Parallel resistance and branch currents
Series-parallel reduction
Current and voltage checks
Power checks

Coming out of this chapter, students can: solve a network and prove the solution with voltage, current, resistance, and power checks.
Suggested work: Assignment 3: series-parallel design proof.
Reference: [1, Chs. 4–6]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
section: 4. Kirchhoff’s laws and systems of equations
text:
4. Kirchhoff’s laws and systems of equations
Learning goal: Apply Kirchhoff’s current law at nodes and Kirchhoff’s voltage law around loops; write, solve, and check two- and three-variable linear systems.
Why it matters: Many real circuits cannot be solved with one equation.
Subsections:

Systems of linear equations
Kirchhoff’s current law
Kirchhoff’s voltage law
Matrices
Residual and power checks

Coming out of this chapter, students can: translate a physical network into simultaneous equations and verify the solution by hand and with software.
Suggested work: Assignment 4: branch-current system solved by hand and checked with software.
References: [1, Chs. 7, 9] [28, Chs. 9, 12]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
5. Equivalent circuits and optimization
Learning goal: Use voltage and current dividers, Thévenin and Norton equivalent circuits, source and load models, maximum power transfer, constraints, and sensitivity.
Why it matters: A simpler model makes a complex design easier to compare and improve.
Subsections:

Voltage and current dividers
Thévenin and Norton equivalents
Source and load models
Maximum power transfer
Constraints
Sensitivity

Coming out of this chapter, students can: recommend a design and defend it using a model, constraints, evidence, and trade-offs.
Suggested work: Assignment 5: source and load optimization memo.
References: [1, Ch. 10] [28, Chs. 13–16]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
6. Material and energy balances
Learning goal: Draw a system boundary and calculate material or energy input, output, accumulation, loss, and efficiency.
Why it matters: A balance shows where material or energy goes and what is being lost.
Subsections:

System boundaries
Process variables
Material balances
Energy balances
Accumulation
Efficiency

Coming out of this chapter, students can: complete an energy audit or supervised low-voltage thermal investigation and explain the losses.
Related TEJ resources: Power and Energy and Computer Power and Parts
Suggested work: Assignment 6: energy audit; Lab 1: supervised low-voltage thermal balance.
References: [1, Chs. 1, 12] [27, Chs. 3, 5–6]






ImportantSafety boundary



Use only teacher-approved protected low-voltage equipment. Students do not construct or probe mains circuits. Isolate liquids from exposed electronics and define temperature, current, containment, and shutdown limits before testing.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
7. Resistor-capacitor and thermal transients
Learning goal: Model resistor-capacitor charging and discharging or heating and cooling using transient response, time constants, and numerical stepping.
Why it matters: Real systems do not change instantly. Time constants also explain how circuits smooth noisy signals and why temperature sensors respond gradually.
Subsections:

Transient response
Resistor-capacitor charging and discharging
Time constants
Signal smoothing and filtering
Thermal response and sensor lag
Numerical stepping and model stability

Coming out of this chapter, students can: model a changing electrical or thermal system and explain how a resistor-capacitor network can smooth a sensor signal.
Suggested work: Assignment 7: resistor-capacitor or thermal transient model.
References: [1, Chs. 16, 18–22] [28, Ch. 25]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
8. Sensors, measurement, calibration, and uncertainty
Learning goal: Select and calibrate sensors; collect repeatable data; report range, sensitivity, resolution, accuracy, repeatability, error, and uncertainty.
Why it matters: Measurements are useful only when students know how much to trust them.
Subsections:

Sensor selection and operating range
Signal conditioning and data acquisition
Calibration
Sensitivity and resolution
Accuracy and repeatability
Error and uncertainty

Coming out of this chapter, students can: calibrate a sensor, graph its response, quantify error, and state where the model is valid.
Instrumentation and data branch: This chapter and the next connect physical measurements to curve fitting, regression, and machine learning.
Suggested work: Lab 2: sensor calibration and model check.
References: [1, Ch. 8] [28, Chs. 3–4]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
section: 9. Curve fitting, regression, and machine learning
text:
9. Curve fitting, regression, and machine learning
Learning goal: Fit and compare models using sensor data, least-squares curve fitting, linear regression, residuals, training and test data, baselines, prediction error, and simple classification.
Why it matters: A model can find useful patterns in data, but it must be tested before it is trusted.
Subsections:

Cleaning and plotting sensor data
Curve fitting and least squares
Linear regression and residuals
Training, validation, and test data
Baselines and model evaluation
Introductory classification
Overfitting, bias, privacy, and limits

Coming out of this chapter, students can: fit a model to non-personal sensor data, measure its error, compare it with a baseline, and explain its limits.
Related TEJ resources: Data Science and Machine Learning
Suggested work: Sensor-data modelling investigation using at least two candidate models and a held-out test set.
References: [28, Chs. 17, 20] [4]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
10. Motors and electromechanical systems
Learning goal: Calculate force, torque, rotational speed, electrical input power, mechanical output power, efficiency, and operating limits.
Why it matters: These calculations show how electrical energy produces useful motion.
Subsections:

Force and motion
Torque
Rotational speed
Electrical power
Mechanical power
Efficiency

Coming out of this chapter, students can: characterize an actuator and explain how load affects current, speed, temperature, and efficiency.
Suggested work: Lab 3: actuator characterization.
Reference: [1, Chs. 13–14]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
section: 11. Boolean logic, algorithms, and state machines
text:
11. Boolean logic, algorithms, and state machines
Learning goal: Use Boolean operators, logic gates, truth tables, algorithms, conditions, programs, state diagrams, and test cases.
Why it matters: These tools turn rules and decisions into systems that can be tested.
Subsections:

Boolean logic
Truth tables
Algorithms
Data structures
State machines
Testing

Coming out of this chapter, students can: create a calculation program or safe state-machine design with documented tests.
Computer-engineering branch: Chapters 11–13 connect logic states, physical outputs, and digital number representation.
Related TEJ resources: Digital Logic and Stable Inputs
Suggested work: Assignment 8: engineering calculation program; Assignment 9: safety state machine; Digital Inputs worksheet.
Reference: [28, Ch. 2]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
12. Sensor, logic, and actuator project
Learning goal: Combine sensor inputs, thresholds, Boolean expressions, truth tables, or state rules to control a motor, fan, relay, alarm, or indicator through a suitable driver circuit.
Why it matters: This project joins sensing, decision making, and physical action in one working system.
Subsections:

Input requirements and sensor thresholds
Stable inputs and signal conditioning
Truth table and Boolean expression
Output driver and flyback protection
Motor, relay, alarm, or indicator output
Safe states and interlocks
Test cases and fault handling

Coming out of this chapter, students can: build or simulate a system that reads sensor states, applies documented logic, and safely controls a physical output.
Related TEJ resources: Digital Logic and Stable Inputs and Control Systems and Computer Numerical Control
Suggested work: Project: sensor-controlled motor, fan, relay, alarm, or indicator with a truth table, schematic, safe output driver, tests, and short explanation.
Safety: Use teacher-approved low-voltage equipment, motor or relay drivers, current limiting, and flyback protection where required.
References: [1, Chs. 13–14] [28, Ch. 2]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
13. Number systems and digital representation
Learning goal: Represent values in binary, decimal, and hexadecimal; interpret bits, bytes, words, Boolean values, signed and unsigned integers, two’s complement, fixed-point and floating-point numbers, range, resolution, and overflow.
Why it matters: A computer can only store a limited pattern of bits, so the representation determines which values it can use and what can go wrong.
Subsections:

Binary, decimal, and hexadecimal
Bits, bytes, and words
Boolean values
Unsigned integers
Signed integers and two’s complement
Fixed-point and floating-point representation
Range, resolution, quantization, and overflow

Coming out of this chapter, students can: convert common number representations, choose a suitable data type, and predict range, resolution, and overflow problems.
Related TEJ resources: Number Systems and Digital Logic and Stable Inputs
Suggested work: Digital representation worksheet using sensor readings, integer ranges, hexadecimal values, and overflow cases.
Reference: [1]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
14. Feedback and control systems
Learning goal: Compare open-loop, on-off, hysteresis, proportional, integral, and derivative control using rise time, overshoot, steady-state error, stability, and saturation.
Why it matters: Feedback helps a system correct itself, but poor settings can make it slow or unstable.
Subsections:

Open-loop control
Feedback
Process control
Response
Stability
Saturation
Safety

Coming out of this chapter, students can: compare control methods using common graphs, response measures, and safety criteria.
Related TEJ resources: Control Systems and Computer Numerical Control
Suggested work: Assignment 10: control-method comparison using the Control Methods Comparison handout.
References: [27, Ch. 3] [28, Chs. 16, 20]

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
15. Engineering design project
Learning goal: Write requirements; create a model, schematic, and program; select sensors and actuators; build or simulate; test, validate, and revise.
Why it matters: The project shows that students can combine the course skills into one working system.
Subsections:

Requirements
Engineering design
Prototype
Experiment
Validation
Optimization
Technical communication

Coming out of this chapter, students can: deliver an instrumented system supported by a mathematical model, test evidence, revision, and a concise technical report.
Suggested project: Instrumented low-voltage thermal process controller. Alternatives may use a motor or pump test stand, battery and thermal monitor, controlled fan, tank-level simulator, or renewable-energy demonstrator.
Deliverable: Requirements, model, schematic, build or approved simulation, code, validation, revision, and concise technical report.

title: Engineering Preparation Track
text:
Core references
The textbooks are teacher references. Public activities use original explanations, diagrams, values, and questions.
[1] Grob’s Basic Electronics, 12th edition supports electronics, measurement, circuit analysis, energy, electromagnetism, and transient circuits.
[4] National Institute of Standards and Technology, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework supports responsible model evaluation, risk analysis, transparency, and human oversight.
[27] Çengel, Introduction to Thermodynamics and Heat Transfer, 2nd edition supports units, energy balances, closed systems, control volumes, heat transfer, and transient thermal behaviour.
[28] Chapra and Canale, Numerical Methods for Engineers, 6th edition supports modelling, error, linear systems, optimization, curve fitting, programming, and numerical time-step models.

title: H09 Series Circuits A
text:
What students learn
Students identify a series circuit as one continuous path, calculate total resistance and current, calculate each voltage drop, check the result with Kirchhoff’s voltage law, and apply resistor power ratings.

title: H09 Series Circuits A
text:
Why it matters
Series analysis lets students predict a circuit before they build it, check measurements, and recognize when a result cannot be correct.

title: H09 Series Circuits A
text:
Learning route

Show a complete low-voltage series system before introducing equations.
Watch the short conceptual introduction and predict what one open component will do.
Move from the physical build to the schematic.
Compare one series path with parallel branches.
Learn the current, resistance, voltage, and power rules.
Complete one guided GUESS example with separate Given and Unknown sections.
Enter each calculator step on a separate line.
Complete five progressively harder questions and submit one photo for each.
Verify the rules with the adapted Grob Experiment 4-1 circuit.

title: H09 Series Circuits A
text:
Experiment 4-1 adaptation
Use a current-limited 10.0 V direct-current supply, a breadboard, a fused digital multimeter, test leads, jumper wires, and 1.0 kΩ, 2.2 kΩ, and 3.3 kΩ resistors. No software is required; Tinkercad can be used as an optional pre-lab.
Students calculate and measure total resistance, current at four points, each voltage drop, the voltage-law check, and percent difference. They submit one clear circuit photo.
Power must be off for resistance measurements. The ammeter must be connected in series. Do not create a deliberate hard short.
Open the Grob Experiments Manual
Experiment 4-2 is a useful resistance-focused extension after the core investigation.

title: SQ06 Repair, Reuse, File Recovery, and Advanced Commissioning
text:
Pathway: Side Quest
Prerequisites: CS06 and one earlier Side Quest
Previous: SQ05 Power and thermal behaviour
Next: Microcontrollers
Define the user need and current machine condition. Choose one teacher-approved scope: return to service, upgrade proposal, approved file recovery, or responsible reuse plan.
Compare safety, workload, cost, data/privacy, energy, expected life, repairability, and parts availability. Build a bill of materials and test plan before changing hardware or data. Repeat acceptance tests after the work.
Follow school data-handling and e-waste procedures. Do not reuse damaged power parts or unknown batteries. Mount recovery drives only as directed.
Submit the decision table, bill of materials, service log, acceptance results, user handoff, remaining risks, and disposition of removed parts.

title: SQ04 Linux Hardware Inventory and Introductory Administration
text:
Pathway: Side Quest
Prerequisite: CS06
Previous: SQ03 Storage and expansion
Next: SQ05 Power and thermal behaviour
Predict which layer can report CPU, RAM, storage, USB, network, and temperature information. Use only teacher-approved commands, which may include lscpu, free -h, lsblk, lspci, lsusb, ip address, smartctl, and sensors.
Capture the command and relevant output rather than the entire terminal history. Compare physical labels, firmware records, and Linux results. Explain one disagreement and produce a concise workstation inventory.
Administrative changes require separate approval. Treat a failing drive or health warning as evidence for caution, not dependable storage.

title: SQ02 Teacher-Prepared POST and Hardware Fault Stations
text:
Pathway: Side Quest
Prerequisite: CS05
Previous: SQ01 Teardown
Next: SQ03 Storage and expansion
The teacher prepares every fault and records the known baseline. Possible stations include improperly seated RAM, disconnected storage, wrong boot order, or an approved fan connection issue.
Record the symptom before touching the station. Predict the normal result, list two possible causes, choose one safe test, make only the approved correction, and verify return to baseline.






ImportantNo student-created faults



Never create a short, damage a connector, invent a fault, or change hardware while power is connected.


Submit the prediction, hypothesis/test log, correction, and verified result.

title: Make It Print
text:
Prerequisites: Power Circuits Questions 1-6 complete, teacher approval, and printer availability.
Use the teacher-approved workflow to print an approved PCSS logo model, if your teacher provides one, or another small teacher-approved object. You do not need to design a new model.

title: Make It Print
text:
Safe workflow

Obtain the printer login from your teacher.
Select the approved printer and model.
Confirm scale, orientation, material, and estimated print time.
Show the sliced preview to the teacher and obtain approval.
Start the print and observe the first layer.
Stop and notify the teacher for poor adhesion, filament problems, unusual noise, collision, smoke, smell, or unexpected movement.
Let the printer and print surface cool, remove the object only when approved, and clean the area.

text:
Evidence
Submit the sliced-preview screenshot, first-layers photo, completed or safely stopped print photo, one statement about what worked, and one improvement for next time.

title: CS08 Build-the-Best-Computer Benchmarking Challenge
text:
Pathway: Main Quest
Prerequisites: CS01-CS07
Previous: CS07 RAM upgrade
Next: Side Quest Hub



A repeatable benchmark and improvement loop.


Define what best means for the assigned user before final testing. Record hardware, operating system, benchmark version, run conditions, units, and baseline results. Use evidence to identify a bottleneck and propose an approved compatible change.
Formal benchmarking begins after the system is operational. USB live-session boot time is a deployment check, not a fair benchmark. An approved storage improvement may be included when equipment is available, but an SSD installation is not required. SQ03 remains the deeper storage and expansion Side Quest.
After the change, complete the inspection gate and rerun the same tests under identical conditions. Report boot/login time, a CPU task, a memory task, a storage task, temperature evidence, and one real user task such as loading Tinkercad or opening Inkscape.
Submit the build plan, parts record, before/after table, graph, uncertainty note, and evidence-based recommendation.
Download the complete student activity package.

title: CS06 Approved Linux Installation and Commissioning
text:
Installation gate
Record the assigned asset, exact target drive model/capacity, preserved files, approved installer, and firmware detection. The teacher must confirm any erase or partition choice.
Use the live session first to test display, keyboard, mouse, USB, Ethernet, Wi-Fi, sound, and storage visibility. After approval, install the operating system selected by the classroom comparison pilot, apply approved updates, and verify CPU, RAM, storage, USB, sound, display, network, restart, and login.






ImportantData safety



An erase-disk installation destroys data on the selected drive. Confirm the exact target and preserve required files before continuing.


The pilot decision is provisional until both Xubuntu 26.04 LTS and Linux Mint Xfce have been tested in the crossover comparison. The teacher may select Xubuntu, Mint Xfce, Lubuntu for weak machines, or additional testing. Ubuntu Server remains reserved for a later dedicated SSH and systems-administration machine.
Official references: Xubuntu releases, Linux Mint downloads, and Ubuntu bootable USB guidance.

title: CS04 Ready-to-Power Inspection and First Boot
text:
Pathway: Main Quest
Prerequisite: CS03
Previous: CS03 Computer power and connections
Next: CS05 POST and BIOS/UEFI

title: CS04 Ready-to-Power Inspection and First Boot
text:
Ready-to-power gate
Check for loose metal, seating, connector alignment, secure cooling, cable clearance, external display/keyboard, and a stable chassis. The teacher must inspect and sign before power is applied.
Predict lights, fan motion, display messages, and sounds. During the supervised boot, record the actual order and compare it with the prediction.






ImportantStop conditions

title: C10 CNC as a Control System
text:
A CNC machine combines a controller, motor drives, axes, home and limit switches, spindle or tool control, coordinate systems, work offsets, G-code, and motion planning.
Open-loop stepper systems assume commanded steps produced motion. Closed-loop servo systems measure motion and correct error. Both architectures need homing, limits, interlocks, and an emergency-stop strategy suitable for the machine.
LinuxCNC provides G-code interpretation, real-time motion control, hardware connections through HAL, and support for open-loop stepper or closed-loop servo systems. Review the official LinuxCNC architecture.

title: C08 Safety Controls and Interlocks
text:
Safety controls should move the system toward a safe state when a stop is pressed, a guard opens, a limit is reached, or a healthy control wire breaks.
Topics include normally closed stop circuits, emergency-stop principles, guard and door interlocks, limit switches, fault states, and fail-safe design.

title: C08 Safety Controls and Interlocks
text:
Classroom model analysis
Draw and explain these states:

normal operation
stop pressed
guard open
limit reached
control wire broken
reset requested while the unsafe condition remains







WarningIndustrial safety boundary



Classroom models teach concepts. Certified industrial safety systems require formal risk assessment, approved components, validated architecture, documentation, and qualified supervision.

title: C06 Integral, Derivative, and PID Control
text:
Integral action responds to accumulated error and can remove steady-state error. Derivative action responds to how quickly error changes and can reduce overshoot when measurements are sufficiently clean.
For a sampled spreadsheet or simulator:
\[u_k=K_Pe_k+K_I\sum_{j=0}^{k}e_j\Delta t+K_D\frac{e_k-e_{k-1}}{\Delta t}\]
This finite-difference form does not require calculus.
Integral windup occurs when error keeps accumulating while the output is saturated. Limit or pause the accumulation as part of the simulation.

title: C06 Integral, Derivative, and PID Control
text:
Manual tuning sequence

Begin with every gain at zero.
Increase \(K_P\) until the response is useful.
Add a small \(K_I\) to remove remaining error.
Add \(K_D\) only when the data quality supports it.
Compare graphs after every change.

Download the required PID comparison activity. A physical PID build is optional.

title: C04 On-Off Control and Hysteresis
text:
On-off control applies full output or zero output. A single threshold can produce rapid switching when noise or process lag moves the measurement around the setpoint.
Hysteresis uses two thresholds. For heating with setpoint \(r\) and half-band \(h\):
With \(r=22^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(h=1^\circ\mathrm{C}\), heat turns on below \(21^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and turns off above \(23^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

title: C04 On-Off Control and Hysteresis
text:
Investigation
Compare \(h=0\), \(0.5\), and \(1.0^\circ\mathrm{C}\) using the same simulated room. Graph temperature and heater state. Discuss cycling frequency, temperature variation, and actuator wear.

title: C02 Open-Loop Control
text:
Open-loop control sends a command without measuring whether the process reached the intended result.
Examples include timed motor operation, fixed PWM, simple conveyor timing, toaster timers, and stepper systems without position feedback.

title: C02 Open-Loop Control
text:
Investigation

Predict motor speed for a fixed \(60\%\) command.
Add a load disturbance halfway through the run.
Plot command and measured speed.
Explain why the controller cannot correct the speed drop.
Identify one situation where open-loop control remains appropriate.

Open loop can be simple, inexpensive, and repeatable when load and environment remain predictable. Its main limitation is the absence of automatic correction.

title: 11. Microcontrollers and Physical Computing
text:
This planned strand begins after students complete digital voltage levels, pull resistors, active-low logic, debouncing, GPIO compatibility, the circuits culminating project, and the required programming foundations.
Planned device pathways include Arduino-compatible boards, Raspberry Pi, micro:bit, and other available controllers. Every activity must identify the exact board, GPIO voltage, current limits, and protection requirements rather than assuming all devices behave alike.
The first physical-computing activity will reuse the same active-low switch circuit from the D01 module so students can separate hardware behaviour from code behaviour.
See the full planned module sequence in the curriculum roadmap.

Reliable table method

For \(n\) inputs, create \(2^n\) rows.
Count upward in binary. The rightmost input changes every row.
Evaluate any NOT operations first.

title: 3.5 Internal Pull-Ups, Debouncing, and Protection
3.5 Internal Pull-Ups, Debouncing, and Protection
3.5 Internal Pull-Ups, Debouncing, and Protection
text:
Contact bounce
Mechanical contacts can produce several rapid transitions during one press. Debounce with a timed software state machine, an RC network connected to a suitable threshold input, or a dedicated circuit.
\[\tau=RC\]



An RC pull-up network filters rapid transitions before the GPIO input.

title: 3.5 Internal Pull-Ups, Debouncing, and Protection
text:
Protection and compatibility
A series resistor and clamp network can limit abnormal current, but it does not turn every 5 V signal into a safe 3.3 V input. Check thresholds, absolute maximum ratings, clamp-current limits, power sequencing, wiring length, and the signal source.






Warning3.3 V and 5 V warning



Do not imply that all GPIO pins are 5 V tolerant. Confirm the exact board, processor, shield, and sensor before connection.

title: 3.3 External Pull-Down Resistors
text:
A pull-down resistor connects the input weakly to ground. The input reads low while the switch is open. Closing the switch connects the input to \(V_{CC}\) and produces a high state.
The GPIO input draws very little current. The pull-down supplies a defined idle state without significantly loading the signal.

title: 3.3 External Pull-Down Resistors
text:
Verification

Predict both states.
Calculate any current path that exists when the switch closes.
Draw the schematic with a junction dot at the input node.
Verify pin voltage for both states.
Disconnect the resistor and document the floating-input limitation.

title: 3.1 Digital Voltage Levels and Logic States
text: Digital inputs measure voltage. The input circuit compares the pin voltage with thresholds specified by the device manufacturer.

title: 3.1 Digital Voltage Levels and Logic States
text:
Compatibility check

Identify the receiving device supply and GPIO domain.
Find guaranteed input-high and input-low thresholds.
Check absolute maximum pin voltage.
Check whether the source remains valid while the receiving device is unpowered.
Select an approved direct connection, divider, buffer, or level shifter.

Raspberry Pi documentation describes its general-purpose header pins as 3.3 V GPIO and warns against using 5 V for 3.3 V components. A nearby 5 V power pin does not make an input 5 V tolerant. See the official Raspberry Pi GPIO documentation.






WarningHardware boundary



Check the exact board and processor. Do not generalize one Arduino, Raspberry Pi, micro:bit, or other microcontroller specification to another device.

title: 2.4 Power & Energy
text:
Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer. It is represented by P and measured in watts (W). [1, pp. 86-93]
P = V × I
One watt is one joule per second:
1 W = 1 J/s
Power supplies are rated in watts because they must deliver energy quickly enough for all of the connected loads.

title: 2.4 Power & Energy
text:
Device labels give useful information
Grob uses appliance nameplates as a practical example: if voltage and power are listed, current can be calculated with I = P / V. [1, p. 98]
We can do the same thing with computer hardware and USB devices.

Example
A USB device operates at:

5.00 V
0.900 A

P = V × I
P = 5.00 V × 0.900 A = 4.50 W
The answer has 3 significant figures.

title: 2.4 Power & Energy
text:
Energy
Power tells us how fast energy is transferred. Energy tells us how much total has been transferred.
E = P × t
For two USB devices drawing 12.00 W for 2.00 h:
E = 12.00 W × 2.00 h = 24.0 Wh
That is also:
86.4 kJ

title: 2.4 Power & Energy
text:
Power supply vs battery
Keep these ideas separate:

a power-supply rating in watts describes a rate of energy delivery
a battery capacity in watt-hours describes an amount of stored energy

title: 2.4 Power & Energy
text:
Inside a computer
Modern electronics repeatedly convert and stabilize power.
Open Circuits shows that multilayer ceramic capacitors are commonly used for local power-supply stability, and it also shows compact DC-DC converter modules that change one DC voltage into another more efficiently than a simple linear regulator. [2, pp. 36, 249]
This gives us a path into later topics:
power -> voltage conversion -> capacitors and inductors -> real motherboard power circuits






TipImprove these notes



Add the voltage, current, or power rating from a real computer component or USB device and show one calculation.

title: 2.2 Closed, Open & Short Circuits
text:
A basic electric circuit needs:

a source that creates a potential difference
a conductive path
a load that uses or transforms electrical energy
a path back to the source

A closed circuit has a complete path, so current can flow. [1, pp. 40-42]

title: 2.2 Closed, Open & Short Circuits
text:
A basic electric circuit needs:

a source that creates a potential difference
a conductive path
a load that uses or transforms electrical energy
a path back to the source

A closed circuit has a complete path, so current can flow. [1, pp. 40-42]

title: 2.2 Closed, Open & Short Circuits
text:
Open circuit
An open circuit has a break in the path.
In the ideal model:

current is 0 A
resistance across the break is treated as extremely high
voltage can still exist across the open gap

Grob uses a simple 10 V circuit to show that opening the path stops current everywhere in that series path. [1, p. 96]
Open circuits can be intentional or accidental:

an open switch
a disconnected cable
a broken wire or PCB trace
a failed component
a blown fuse







ImportantTroubleshooting idea



No current does not automatically mean no voltage.
An open circuit can still have the applied voltage across the break.

title: 2.2 Closed, Open & Short Circuits
text:
Short circuit
A short circuit creates a path with very low resistance.
Ohm’s law predicts that, for a given voltage, lower resistance allows more current:
I = V / R
Real wires and sources never have exactly zero resistance, but a short can still allow enough current to overheat wiring or damage components. [1, pp. 96-97]

title: 2.2 Closed, Open & Short Circuits
text:
Fuses intentionally create an open
A fuse protects a circuit by opening the path if the current becomes too high.
Open Circuits shows cartridge fuses in which a metal element heats and melts when current exceeds the fuse rating. [2, pp. 54-58]
The sequence is:
excess current -> heating -> fuse element opens -> current stops
A blown fuse is usually evidence of another problem. Find the cause before simply replacing the fuse.

title: 2.2 Closed, Open & Short Circuits
section: Switches are controlled opens and closes
text:
Switches are controlled opens and closes
A normally open pushbutton has a deliberate break in the circuit until it is pressed. Pressing the button moves a metal contact into place and completes the circuit. [2, p. 109]
This gives us a useful mental model:

open switch -> path broken
closed switch -> path complete

title: 2.2 Closed, Open & Short Circuits
text:
Measurement reminder
Measure resistance with the circuit power off. A voltage can remain across an open circuit even when no current is flowing. [1, pp. 95-96]

title: 2.2 Closed, Open & Short Circuits
text:
Quick check
For each situation, predict the current and explain why:

a switch is open
a switch is closed
a wire directly connects the positive and negative sides of a low-voltage source
a fuse has blown
a USB cable has an internal broken conductor

Add a real troubleshooting example of an open or short circuit.

title: 1.1 Significant Figures
text:
Significant figures communicate the precision of a measured or stated value.

Non-zero digits are significant.
Zeros between significant digits are significant.
Leading zeros are not significant.
Trailing zeros are significant when the notation makes the precision clear.
In scientific notation, the coefficient makes the intended significant figures clear.

Examples:
42.7 has 3 significant figures. 0.00420 has 3 significant figures.

title: 1.1 Significant Figures
text:
Calculations

Adding and subtracting
Round the answer to the least precise decimal place.
16.3 + 17.14 = 33.44 → 33.4


Multiplying and dividing
Round the answer to the same number of significant figures as the value with the fewest significant figures.
6.23 × 1.23 = 7.6629 → 7.66 (3 significant figures)
Keep full calculator precision through the calculation and round once, at the end.

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
text:
FROM THE ARCHIVE
Originally published on andrewandrade.ca. This version is included in Lore because it captures the kind of learning record this section is meant to preserve: teaching, history, identity, community, and the things carried forward.
View the source history on GitHub
It’s been years since I last wrote here. I started this blog back in fourth-year engineering while job hunting, before I joined Palantir, before robotics labs and late-night debugging sessions, before teaching, before all the twists that came after.
This week, Remembrance Day brought me back.
I had the honour of playing trumpet with our school band, not the Last Post; I’m still working to be good enough for that, but enough to stand with the group in something meaningful. Instruments in hand, everything paused for a moment, and it pulled me right back to my time in army cadets.
Even now, that first year is burned into my memory: awkward uniform, barely any badges, trying to figure out what leadership meant. Luckily we had mentors to guide us.
Cadets taught me that rank wasn’t the patch; it was the work behind it.
As we approached Remembrance Day this year, I found myself thinking about the small rituals that shaped me. Raising the flag was one of them.
Sometimes it was early, cold, or rushed, but it mattered. And I wasn’t alone.
Music also became part of those mornings, including our national anthem.
Fast-forward to high school robotics, coding, and engineering, different worlds entirely, but the same threads of discipline and responsibility ran through them.
I didn’t stay long enough in cadets to stack up badges like the mentors I admired, but the two years I spent there were full. Varied, intense, and formative, but I still loved computers.
This year, as part of preparing for our ceremony, I learned more than I expected, thanks entirely to the Student Activity Council, who did all the research.
That’s where I discovered the story of George Cardozo, one of the “Port Credit Boys.”

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
section: The Bugler They Didn’t Let Become an Officer
text:
The Bugler They Didn’t Let Become an Officer
George’s story starts decades before mine, but strangely close to home.
He was a Jamaican-born teacher, educated in Port-au-Prince and Kingston, who came to Canada and enlisted with the 4th Battalion, Canadian Expeditionary Force, on 22 September 1914.
One of the first recruits at Valcartier.



George standing


His attestation paper recorded only the essentials: his trade or calling, his date of birth, and his place of birth. Beyond those brief entries, the rest of George’s life, identity, and service must be reconstructed through the surviving evidence gathered from archival and family research.
A fuller picture, his experiences as a Jamaican-born bugler, his movement through the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and the context surrounding his enlistment, comes from the sources compiled in the project’s research. These include My Jamaican Family’s biography They Shall Grow Not Old: George Cardozo, a Casualty of …, the Canadian Virtual War Memorial entry for George Cordozo from Veterans Affairs Canada, and his digitized service file in Library and Archives Canada’s Personnel Records of the First World War.
Together, these sources allow us to understand George far more deeply than the minimal information captured on the photo.



George’s attestation paper


According to Dorothy Kew from the My Jamaican Family Blog, he was:

Five foot five
Dark complexion
“Coloured”
Roman Catholic
Teacher

With his education and background, he should have been an officer.
But because of his colour, he wasn’t given that chance.
Instead, they made him a bugler.



George sitting


Today, the role is ceremonial.
Back then, buglers woke before everyone else, played Reveille in the cold, roused officers, and handled the morning chores no one else wanted.
George still trained hard, at Ravina Barracks, on the SS Tyrolia to England, and finally to the Western Front.



Port Credit Boys


He died sometime between April 22 and 26, 1915, during the Second Battle of Ypres, the first time poison gas was used in the Great War. His body was never found.
His name is carved on the Menin Gate Memorial in Belgium with over 55,000 others who have no known grave.



Memorial


Every evening at 8 p.m., beneath his name, they still sound the Last Post.

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
section: Bugles, Flags, and the Things We Carry Forward
text:
Bugles, Flags, and the Things We Carry Forward
This year I raised my trumpet high,
Not for the Last Post’s mournful cry,
But with a deeper, steadier sight
Of all the threads that shaped my flight.
I thought of flags I used to raise,
The badges missed in younger days,
The mentors’ paths I didn’t tread,
And those who served and marched instead.
I thought of George, so much like me,
A teacher-learner meant to be,
Who left to fight through smoke and flame
And never made it home again.

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
text:
We Remember

“They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old…”
- For the Fallen, Lawrence Binyon

This post is both a return and a reminder, of the past we inherit, the stories we uncover, and the unexpected ways they shape our present.
This Remembrance Day, I played the trumpet for our school.
But I also played it for George.
And I’m honoured to remember him here.

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
section: Choose the support by the force path
text:
Choose the support by the force path

Straight tabbed pair: locates two members in the front plane. It still needs a separate base that provides front-to-back depth.
Angled tabbed pair: spreads the feet sideways in the front view. It still needs a separate base or rear support for front-to-back stability.
Triangular side cheeks: can carry a plaque between two side panels, but this generator does not create the required joints.
Wide single easel back: generates a T-shaped support plus optional mating-slot geometry. A fixed slot connection is not the same as a hinge.
Narrow hinged rear strut: is one component of a picture-frame-style easel. It needs a front plaque, pivot hardware and a tether or stop.
Interlocking X-base: generates two half-slotted base bars only. The upright and plaque connection must be designed separately.

The purple coupon tests the chosen tab length and calculated slot width. Blue slot rectangles are mating geometry to position in the holder plate, not separate finished parts.

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
text:
Before cutting

Measure the actual sheet thickness in several places.
Cut the fit coupon before the complete legs.
Open the SVG in Inkscape and confirm its physical dimensions at 100% scale.
Place matching slots in the holder plate and check that each slot has enough material around it.
Prototype in cardboard or scrap stock.
Assemble the real holder and test front-to-back and side-to-side tipping.

Read Make It Stand for the easel force diagrams, bending explanation, starting proportions and external reference templates. Use the Fabrication Plate Builder for the holder plate and repeated holes.

title: Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder
section: Which reference file do I use?
text:
Which reference file do I use?
The SVG, DXF, DWG, CDR, PDF and PNG in the reference folder are different formats of the same template set. Do not combine all six files.

Use SVG in Inkscape. This is the easiest editable version for the laser workflow.
Use DXF or DWG in CAD/CAM software when that program handles those formats better.
Use CDR only in CorelDRAW.
Use PDF or PNG to look at or print the design. They are reference views, not the preferred editable cut file.

The external sheet contains several easel concepts. Select one complete matching group of parts, move that group into a new document, confirm the scale, and resize every slot for the measured sheet thickness. The reference was drawn around 0.118-inch material, which is slightly thinner than nominal 1/8-inch material. Always test one joint first.

Ontario Broad-Based Technological Education · Reusable curriculum

This open pathway helps students move from a real need to a communicated idea, a measured prototype, and an improved fabricated result. It connects design with digital communication and fabrication without treating any one technology area, or any one machine, as the default context.

title: General Design & Fabrication
text:
Complete shop pathway



Broad design and fabrication reference


Systems Design & Fabrication Track


Connect N.I.C.E. with orthographic drawings, standards, GD&T, fits, machine design, fasteners and concrete anchors, wood and sheet preparation, metal cutting, separate MIG/TIG/stick/spot welding sections, milling, turning, grinding, CNC, laser cutting, 3D printing, plasma cutting, production systems and an integrated capstone.

title: General Design & Fabrication
text:
Learn



01 · Start here


N.I.C.E. Design Process


Understand the situation, distinguish necessities from nice-to-haves, investigate existing solutions, generate alternatives, communicate a concept, prototype, evaluate, and begin the next iteration.


Learn the design process




02 · Think critically


AI Literacy & Reproducible Workflows


Define criteria before prompting, give AI a limited job, verify claims and sources, protect privacy, iterate because of evidence, and document/disclose meaningful use.


Audit and document AI-assisted work




03 · Communicate


Digital Design & Communication


Build visual literacy through raster/vector graphics, original logos, typography, Pencil2D animation, artistic Blender work, and a small website/UI-UX portfolio.


Build digital design skills




04 · Fabricate in 2D


Laser Cutting & 2D Fabrication


Start with a simple engraved name tag, then select measurement, calibration, fit, supports, assemblies and hybrid-fabrication notes as the project requires.


Learn laser fabrication




05 · Model + fabricate in 3D


3D Modelling + 3D Printing


Contrast Onshape parametric/solid CAD with Blender mesh work, then learn source files, STL/3MF/STEP, slicing, orientation, supports, tolerances and iteration.


Learn modelling and additive manufacturing




06 · Additional methods


CNC, Textiles & Other Fabrication


Extend the same design, drawing, material, process-planning, inspection and iteration habits to CNC/digital machining, textiles/soft goods, vinyl, plasma, sheet metal, forming, molding, casting and composites.


Explore additional fabrication methods

title: General Design & Fabrication
text:
Reusable Ontario technology resources
These lessons can support Ontario secondary school Broad-Based Technological Education in different ways. Teachers can use the whole sequence or select a design process, communication, measurement, or fabrication lesson that fits a local project, technology context, and available equipment.

Ontario curriculum relevance: The complete pathway is especially useful for TIJ1O Exploring Technologies. Individual units also transfer to TDJ, TMJ, TGJ, TEJ, TCJ, THJ, TTJ, TXJ, TFJ, and TPJ contexts where the learning genuinely involves design, measurement, prototyping, communication, or fabrication. The application pages make those connections explicit without claiming one-to-one curriculum expectation mappings.

title: General Design & Fabrication
text:
General notes and course-specific notes
General Design & Fabrication is the canonical reusable layer for N.I.C.E., AI literacy, graphics, animation, UI/UX, parametric CAD, laser fabrication, 3D printing and general organizer guidance. TEJ Notes remain specific to computer engineering/electronics. TTJ/TTS slides and notes remain specific to transportation, automotive and shop learning. Those courses should link here for shared fabrication concepts instead of duplicating this curriculum.

title: Technological Design Project Ideas
text: In Technological Design, the fabricated object is evidence inside a design process. Require a defensible brief, criteria and constraints, alternative concepts, measured drawings or CAD, prototype testing, and a revision, not just a rendered final form.

title: Technological Design Project Ideas
text:
Project directions


Ergonomic shared-tool organizer

TDJ2O / senior TDJ · Organizer family

Improve access for two users with different reach, hand size, or visual needs while keeping an accurate inventory visible.


Process


Observation → anthropometric assumptions → mock-up → parametric CAD → prototype


Skills


Criteria weighting, ergonomics, clearances, technical drawing, user testing


Difficulty / size


Intermediate · desktop module under 350 mm wide


Material


Cardboard proof, then plywood or printed polymer components


Structural


Test tipping, handle load, repeated removal, and replaceable parts


Use boundary


Do not infer accessibility from one user; remove pinch and sharp-edge hazards


Library


Modular organization interfaces


Lesson


Evaluate, Re-question & Iterate


Extension


Publish a parameter table that allows another class to resize the design




Comparative fit-test fixture

TDJ2O / senior TDJ · Gauge family

Create a fixture that isolates one variable (clearance, slot fit, fastener position, or printed tolerance) and records repeatable results.


Process


Define variable → control geometry → fabricate series → measure → graph result


Skills


Experimental design, tolerancing, data visualization, revision control


Difficulty / size


Intermediate · hand-sized coupon series


Material


The same stock or filament planned for the final prototype


Structural


Include datums and labels that survive handling


Use boundary


Test samples are process references, not rated structural coupons


Library


Calibration assets


Lesson


Material Fit + Calibration


Extension


Compare two machines or orientations and explain the different result




Configurable product display

Senior TDJ · Display family

Design a knock-down display whose angle, message panel, or product support can change without remaking the whole system.


Process


Use scenario → mechanism concepts → scale model → full-size critical joint


Skills


Systems thinking, interfaces, assembly sequence, communication drawing


Difficulty / size


Intermediate–advanced · 300–600 mm tall


Material


Sheet stock plus printed connectors or standard fasteners


Structural


State load case, safety factor assumption, and failure mode


Use boundary


Prototype displays only; public installation requires appropriate review


Library


Project components


Lesson


Assemblies + Hybrid Fabrication


Extension


Prepare an exploded view, bill of materials, and end-of-life plan

title: Design & Fabrication Ideas by Technology Area
section: Four project families that transfer well
text:
Four project families that transfer well



Organizer


The same retention-and-access problem becomes a socket rack in TTJ, a cable module in TEJ, a sanitized-tool workflow model in TXJ, or a labelled supply organizer in TPJ. Students measure the actual objects and test reach, visibility, stability, and cleaning access.




Display


A stable display can communicate a brand in TGJ, plant information in THJ, a menu in TFJ, a building detail in TCJ, or a public-health message in TPJ. The audience, viewing distance, accessibility, and environment change the criteria.




Gauge or template


A reference tool may check hole spacing in TMJ, screw length in TCJ, wiring pitch in TEJ, service part size in TTJ, or repeatable label placement in TGJ. It must state exactly what it measures and its limits.




Portable work module


A bounded module makes a complete task visible and movable: electronics test leads, styling consultation materials, field-observation tools, construction layout tools, or event-service information. Handles, centre of mass, inventory, and setup sequence become design evidence.

title: Design & Fabrication Ideas by Technology Area
text:
Use the reference layer responsibly
Each project card names a problem, course context, process, skills, scale, material, structural concern, use boundary, library starting point, lesson link, and extension. These boundaries describe what a classroom prototype is and is not intended to do; they are not machine operating instructions. Treat dimensions as hypotheses until students measure the real object and environment. Course codes identify useful contexts, not official expectation mappings; teachers should connect a chosen project to their current curriculum document and local board requirements.
Machine-specific safety instruction, operating procedures, assessments, and authorization are kept outside this public website. Follow your school board’s safety guidelines and the course-specific instruction provided by your teacher. Students in Mr. Andrade’s classes can find that information in Google Classroom.

title: AI Design Audit | Verify a Fabrication Answer
text:
An AI answer recommends making a laser-cut stand from “1/4-inch plywood,” using a 6.35 mm slot, subtracting 0.2 mm for kerf, and downloading “any free SVG.” It claims the result will press-fit perfectly and be safe on every school laser.
Your job is to audit the answer, not to follow it.

title: AI Design Audit | Verify a Fabrication Answer
text:
An AI answer recommends making a laser-cut stand from “1/4-inch plywood,” using a 6.35 mm slot, subtracting 0.2 mm for kerf, and downloading “any free SVG.” It claims the result will press-fit perfectly and be safe on every school laser.
Your job is to audit the answer, not to follow it.

title: AI Design Audit | Verify a Fabrication Answer
text:
Complete the audit

Mark each statement as fact, assumption or suggestion.
Identify unsupported claims, invented certainty, missing information and safety boundaries.
Measure the actual approved sheet in several places and record the range.
Find the local machine/material instructions and an authoritative explanation of kerf or fit testing.
Explain why material thickness, machine, settings, grain, geometry and desired fit affect the result.
Replace “any free SVG” with a specific source-and-licence check or an original design.
Rewrite the prompt so AI has one limited job and must label uncertainty.
Compare the two outputs against the same criteria.
Design a small fit-test coupon; do not fabricate until the teacher approves the file and process.
Write the final human decision and the evidence still needed after the AI work.

title: AI Design Audit | Verify a Fabrication Answer
text:
Submit
Submit the flawed answer with annotations, verified source record, measurement table, improved prompt and output, comparison, test plan, decision log and AI-use disclosure. The strongest work shows why a suggestion was accepted or rejected and makes no claim that a simulation or answer replaced a physical test.
Continue into Digital Design & Communication or apply the audit to material fit and calibration.

title: Iterate with Purpose | Change the Prompt Because of Evidence
text:
More outputs do not automatically mean more learning. Each meaningful version should answer:

What did the previous output get wrong, miss or leave uncertain?
What new evidence did you add?
What changed in the prompt or process?
What improved, and what still needs a human or physical test?

Keep a compact decision log: version, change, reason, accepted/rejected ideas, evidence and next step. Usually three meaningful versions, or the number set by the teacher, are more useful than a long transcript of nearly identical prompts.
Do not ask AI to “make it better.” Name the failed criterion: “The proposed opening assumes a 10 mm handle, but the measured handles range from 11.8–14.2 mm. Compare one adjustable strategy and two size-family strategies without selecting a clearance.”
Next: Document and disclose AI use.

title: 3D Printing Slicing | Layer Height, Walls, Infill, Orientation & Supports
text: A slicer converts the 3D model into layers and machine instructions. Previewing the toolpath is part of design verification, not an optional final click.

title: 3D Printing Slicing | Layer Height, Walls, Infill, Orientation & Supports
text: A slicer converts the 3D model into layers and machine instructions. Previewing the toolpath is part of design verification, not an optional final click.

title: 3D Printing Slicing | Layer Height, Walls, Infill, Orientation & Supports
text:
Settings with consequences

Layer height: changes vertical detail, surface texture, time, and the number of layer interfaces.
Walls/perimeters: strongly affect shell strength and feature quality.
Infill: supports top surfaces and can change stiffness, mass, and time; more is not automatically better.
Top and bottom layers: close surfaces and distribute loads.
Orientation: changes overhangs, supports, surface finish, dimensional behaviour, and the direction of layer weakness.
Supports: make some overhangs possible but add material, time, cleanup, and surface evidence.

title: 3D Printing Slicing | Layer Height, Walls, Infill, Orientation & Supports
text:
Orientation comparison
Choose a bracket or hook and compare at least three orientations. For each, record support volume, estimated time, contact area, critical surface quality, likely load direction, and risk of failure. Select an orientation against the actual requirements rather than the most attractive preview.

title: 3D Printing Slicing | Layer Height, Walls, Infill, Orientation & Supports
text:
Before printing
Inspect the first layer, thin walls, bridges, unsupported islands, travel, seams, and total material. Confirm the intended printer and material profile. Machine-specific safety instruction and operating procedures follow school board guidelines and the course information provided by the teacher; students in Mr.� Andrade’s classes use Google Classroom for that material.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
Choose an existing tool holder, organizer, fixture, or storage product as a precedent. Study what it does well, identify a real opportunity, then create an original design that improves the experience for a defined user and context.
The goal is not to make a copy. The goal is to learn from a good idea, explain how it works, and produce a better response to the problem using your own measurements, geometry, testing, and documentation.
Your evidence should justify each criterion, make every trade-off visible, and show at least one iteration.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
Choose an existing tool holder, organizer, fixture, or storage product as a precedent. Study what it does well, identify a real opportunity, then create an original design that improves the experience for a defined user and context.
The goal is not to make a copy. The goal is to learn from a good idea, explain how it works, and produce a better response to the problem using your own measurements, geometry, testing, and documentation.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
The design challenge
Develop a tool holder or organizer that improves at least three of these qualities:

Faster: quicker to fabricate, assemble, install, use, inspect, clean, or return tools to.
Cheaper: less material, fewer parts, common hardware, shorter machine time, or lower replacement cost.
Better looking: clearer proportions, stronger visual hierarchy, intentional colour and form, or a better fit with its setting.
More ergonomic: easier reach, a safer grip, better visibility, comfortable clearances, and one-hand use where appropriate.
More positive: creates calm, confidence, pride, delight, belonging, or satisfaction instead of clutter and frustration.
More useful: holds the right objects, supports a wider range, or solves a problem the precedent misses.
More durable or serviceable: stronger load path, replaceable wear parts, accessible fasteners, or easier repair.
More responsible: less waste, fewer mixed materials, efficient sheet layout, or parts that can be reused.

Every gain has a possible trade-off. A cheaper design may take longer to assemble. A smaller design may make tools harder to grasp. State what improved, what did not, and what evidence supports the claim.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
1. Find precedents
Collect at least three references from two different source types. Include one commercial product and one build, model, or assembly that reveals how parts might work together.

Product and laser-project ideas

Etsy tool-holder results: compare use cases, forms, prices, claims, and recurring themes in public reviews. Do not copy seller photos, artwork, or files.
Glowforge Catalog: study laser-cut construction, layer strategies, visual language, and product categories. Catalog access does not grant permission to redistribute or recreate a paid design.
Instructables tool-organizer search: look for build sequences, material choices, mistakes, tests, and revisions.



Mechanisms and fabrication ideas

Printables tool-holder search: inspect mounting, retention, modularity, print orientation, user makes, ratings, and comments.
Thingiverse tool-holder and organization group: compare holders for specific tools with broader workshop systems.
MakerWorld tool-holder collection: study adjustable, magnetic, modular, and low-support approaches.



Assemblies and form studies

Onshape public documents: use the Public filter to study part relationships, assemblies, parameters, and drawings.
Sketchfab tool-holder models: rotate models to inspect form, access, and assembly. Check the licence on each model before downloading or reusing anything.



Graphics and visual language

Openverse, Openclipart, and Noun Project: investigate symbols, silhouettes, and graphic styles for labels. Check the individual licence and attribution requirement before use.

Start locally too: browse the Laser Fabrication Library, purpose-built holder kits, five organizer reference assemblies, and Tool Organizer Gallery.
For more starting points, use the Free Online Design & Fabrication Resource Directory · Work in Progress. It adds provisional notes on inclusive-design references, repair sites, CAD and graphics tools, museum scans, packaging generators, electronics projects, and sustainability resources. A teacher must review each entry before classroom use.






ImportantPublicly visible does not mean free to copy



Record the creator or seller, page title, URL, access date, and stated licence for every reference. You may analyze publicly observable functions, interfaces, proportions, mechanisms, and user feedback. Do not trace product photographs, reproduce logos or distinctive decoration, download files without permission, bypass payment, or present another person’s work as your own. Reuse a file only when its licence clearly permits your intended use, and provide the required attribution.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
section: 2. Reverse engineer the problem, not the artwork
text:
2. Reverse engineer the problem, not the artwork
For each precedent, make an evidence table.







Question
Evidence to record




Who is it for?
User, setting, tools, reach zone, and likely routine


What problem does it solve?
Need, current frustration, and desired result


How does it work?
Support, retention, mounting, labels, load path, and assembly


What looks successful?
Features supported by photographs, specifications, build notes, or repeated review themes


What could improve?
Specific issue, affected user, and evidence rather than a guess


What cannot be confirmed online?
Hidden dimensions, material grade, strength, comfort, fit, or long-term durability



Treat reviews as clues, not facts. Look for repeated observations, separate shipping or seller issues from product-design issues, and verify what you can with direct measurement and testing.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
3. Write an improvement brief
Use this sentence frame:

Design an original [product] for [user and setting] that [solves the need]. It must [three measurable criteria] while respecting [material, machine, time, safety, and cost constraints].

Turn broad intentions into testable criteria.







Intention
Testable version




Faster
A user can identify, remove, and return the selected tool in 10 seconds or less.


Cheaper
The design fits within the assigned sheet area and uses no more than two purchased fastener types.


Better looking
Three users can identify the intended tool group and describe the visual hierarchy without prompting.


More ergonomic
The target tools can be removed with one hand without pinching neighbouring tools or twisting the wrist sharply.


More positive
User feedback includes a chosen feeling, such as calm or confidence, and identifies the feature that created it.


More serviceable
A damaged holder component can be replaced without discarding the backer or removing unrelated tools.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
4. Generate and select concepts

Measure the real tools, mounting area, stock, and critical hand clearances.
Sketch at least three meaningfully different concepts. Changing only decoration does not create a new concept.
Annotate the support method, retention method, mounting interface, assembly order, and expected load path.
Score each concept against the criteria using a decision matrix.
Explain the selected concept and one trade-off you accepted.

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
section: 5. Build evidence before the full product

title: Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
Good Idea, Better Product | Reverse-Engineering Design Challenge
text:
Assessment focus







Area
Evidence of strong work




Investigation
Varied, relevant, attributed precedents and careful interpretation of user evidence


Originality
New geometry and decisions tied to this user, tool set, and context


Improvement
Clear, measurable gains in at least three selected qualities


Technical quality
Accurate measurement, suitable tolerances, efficient layout, and intentional assembly


Testing
A critical question tested early with recorded results and a meaningful revision


Communication
Clear drawings, source links, licences, comparison, and honest claim language

The teacher should select a scope, process, and assessment emphasis appropriate to the course and available equipment. Machine-specific safety information follows school board guidelines and the course information provided by the teacher; students in Mr. Andrade’s classes use Google Classroom for that material.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text: Build the design from measurements and named parts. Do not redraw every primitive by eye. Keep the editable master; make a separate fabrication copy only when the local machine workflow requires converted text or flattened artwork.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Before the screen

Complete the fabrication planning worksheet.
Draw front, top and side views. Mark the datum: the edge or centre from which important dimensions are located.
Measure the real object and sheet. Record ranges when objects vary.
Decide whether each circle means a hole or a circle part.
Identify one critical feature to test before the complete cut.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Set up Inkscape

Open File → Document Properties.
Set display units and document units to mm.
Set the page to the intended physical output size.
Save immediately as project-name_v01_master.svg.
Turn on snapping only when it supports the intended datum and alignment; do not let snapping replace entered dimensions.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Bring in building blocks
If the project begins as a plate with a row, grid, radial or perimeter hole pattern, use the Fabrication Plate Builder first. Its output is intentionally plain: CUT_OUTER, CUT_HOLES and an optional GUIDES group. Inkscape remains the place to add labels, slots, custom profiles and manufacturing intent.

Open the relevant component palette.
Select the named component group and copy it into the master file.
Use the toolbar or Object → Transform to enter exact width, height and position.
Rename the group by purpose: top-shelf, bottle-hole-01, left-gusset.
Duplicate repeated parts from one checked original. Use Object → Align and Distribute for centres and spacing.

Avoid advanced node editing in the first sequence. If a shape requires many uncontrolled node moves, return to simpler parts or revise the paper plan.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Separate manufacturing intent
Use clearly named groups or layers for CUT, SCORE and ENGRAVE. The library uses red, blue and black as a communication convention, but the machine operator confirms the local mapping. A colour alone is never approval to cut.
For the first name-tag engraving, set the page to the measured pre-cut blank, keep artwork inside the safe margin, hide/delete guides, and export the page as PNG at the instructor-set resolution. Reopen the PNG and confirm pixel dimensions, crop and orientation before it enters the laser workflow.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow
text:
Preflight

Page width, page height and intended object size are correct in mm.
Every critical dimension matches the paper plan.
One controlled original was used for duplicates.
No duplicate paths, stray objects, hidden output or critical external fonts remain.
The machine preview contains the expected count of cuts and engraves.
A fit coupon was made for slots, holes, hardware or measured objects.
The filename shows project and version; obsolete versions are not sent accidentally.

title: Paper to Inkscape | Student Workflow

title: Design & Fabrication Capstone | Complete a N.I.C.E. Design Cycle
text:
Required design record

Situation and need: user, context, facts, assumptions, requirements, restrictions, necessities, and priorities.
Inquiry: useful questions, credible sources, existing solutions, comparisons, and opportunities to borrow, combine, adapt, or improve.
Alternatives: distinct concepts with reasons, not cosmetic variations of one idea.
Selected concept: labelled communication, dimensions, materials, process plan, and identified uncertainties.
Prototype: a purposeful model or test for the highest-risk question.
Fabrication: versioned files, settings, material records, safe process, and assembly decisions.
Feedback and testing: observations from realistic use, measurements, and user response.
Evaluation and iteration: evidence compared with the need and a documented next version.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text: Calibration is not one magic kerf value. It is a short, recorded test that connects this sheet, this machine condition, this geometry, and this intended fit.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
Operating procedure or material calibration?



Operating procedure


Machine-specific setup, safety instruction, assessments, and authorization are not provided on this public website. Follow your school board’s safety guidelines and the course-specific instruction provided by your teacher. Students in Mr. Andrade’s classes can find that information in Google Classroom.




Material calibration


Measure how one stock-and-setting combination changes size and fit. This is about the result of the process.



Actual thickness and batch are recorded.


A known drawing dimension imports at 100%.


Cut width and finished dimensions are measured.


Slots and holes are tested against the real mating object.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
1 · Measure the actual sheet
Plywood sold as 1/4 inch may not measure 6.35 mm. Measure at several locations with callipers, including near a visibly damaged edge but not on it. Record the minimum, maximum and the value used to design the test.

Material thicknessRecord a measured range, not a catalogue assumption. Ruler / scale checkConfirm millimetres and 100% import before cutting. Dimension verificationCompare a known drawing dimension to the finished result.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
2 · Understand what kerf changes
The beam removes a narrow band centred on the path. With the path drawn on the intended boundary, an outside part tends to finish smaller and an inside opening tends to finish larger. The magnitude varies, so do not copy a universal number.



Kerf diagram showing the cut band around a vector path, a smaller outside part and a larger inside opening.


BRM’s current kerf and kerf-compensation explanation is a useful process reference. BRM also hosts a free kerf gauge SVG, credited there to Nameek and Elplatt, and explicitly tells users to check scale after import. Use it as another test method, not as a pre-approved local setting.
Ponoko’s 2011 article, Figuring out kerf for precision parts, is included only as a historical/conceptual example of test-and-revise thinking. Do not copy its old settings or service-specific assumptions.

Kerf testMeasure a repeated cut rather than guessing from one edge. Tab fitTest the male feature and its orientation. Slot fitStart from measured thickness, then compare a small series. Four-fit seriesName the function: loose, sliding, snug or press. Hole fitTest the actual bottle, dowel or fastener, not only a calliper.

title: Laser Cutter Calibration | Material Thickness, Kerf & Fit Tests
text:
3 · Cut, measure and decide

Open one test SVG in Inkscape and confirm document units, viewBox scale and a known dimension.
Label the coupon with material, batch, date, machine and revision before cutting.
Use the course-specific process provided by your teacher.
Let the coupon cool and measure it consistently; do not force a calliper into a soft or angled edge.
Test the real mating object in every candidate feature.
Select the fit that serves the function. A press fit is not automatically “more accurate” than a sliding fit.
Update the source dimension, save the record and repeat only the smallest necessary test.







Warning



Kerf compensation changes geometry; it does not correct a machine-condition problem, warped stock, or an incorrectly scaled import. Resolve unexpected machine behaviour through the course-specific process before interpreting the coupon.
