title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text: Create a simple holder for measured classroom objects such as markers, pencils, screwdrivers, drill bits, or small electronics tools. The openings must come from real measurements, not a generic file or guessed diameter.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text:
Measure the object
Use calipers correctly and record units. Measure more than one example when nominally identical objects may vary. Identify the controlling dimension: outside diameter, widest body, collar, taper, handle shape, or removal clearance.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text:
Build the layout

Create one opening from an exact measured dimension.
Decide what clearance the task requires; do not silently treat a nominal measurement as a finished fit.
Duplicate the opening into a controlled row or array.
Set centre-to-centre spacing and edge margins numerically.
Align labels and openings consistently.
Check that the remaining material between openings is strong enough for the intended use.

Use circles, holes, slots, rulers, and spacing templates as editable references. The source geometry is a starting point; the student’s measured object determines the final design.
For the first controlled organizer exercise, compare the Hole, Slot and Organizer palettes. Copy named groups, enter dimensions numerically, and make every repeated opening from one checked original.
Draw front, top and side views on the planning worksheet before building the digital layout. Use the Paper-to-Inkscape workflow for datums, grouping, alignment and preflight.
For a row, grid, staggered, radial or perimeter layout, the Fabrication Plate Builder can turn the checked measurements into a reproducible true-size SVG. It validates boundaries and overlap, but the calibration lesson is still required to decide the finished fit.

title: Measure + Place | Calipers and Exact Geometry for Laser Cutting
text:
Evidence
Submit a measurement table, dimensioned layout, fabrication file, fit observation, and one revision. A visually even layout is not enough if tools bind, fall through, or cannot be removed easily.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Useful for TIJ1O, TMJ2O, TDJ2O, TCJ2O, TEJ2O, and TTJ2O contexts involving measurement, precision, layout, repeated geometry, tool organization, and prototype evaluation.

Next: learn why the measured opening and the cut result can differ in Material Fit + Calibration.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Use the process that best suits each function. Thin laser-cut Baltic birch is valuable for precision faces, tool openings, slots, holes, dividers, shadow-board fronts, engraved labels, retainers, spacers, alignment aids, and drilling templates. It is not automatically the right structural rail or load-bearing backer.
Use 1/2 inch or 3/4 inch plywood, conventional lumber, commercial fasteners, dowels, or other approved materials where stiffness, impact resistance, screw holding, or load capacity matters.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Use the process that best suits each function. Thin laser-cut Baltic birch is valuable for precision faces, tool openings, slots, holes, dividers, shadow-board fronts, engraved labels, retainers, spacers, alignment aids, and drilling templates. It is not automatically the right structural rail or load-bearing backer.
Use 1/2 inch or 3/4 inch plywood, conventional lumber, commercial fasteners, dowels, or other approved materials where stiffness, impact resistance, screw holding, or load capacity matters.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Assembly vocabulary

Floor and walls: establish the main volume and load path.
Tabs and slots: locate parts and transfer forces when sized for actual material.
Pins and dowels: align, hinge, retain, or reinforce.
Screws: allow removable mechanical assembly when the receiving material is suitable.
Glue: bonds compatible surfaces but should not compensate for a poorly fitted or unsafe structure.
Spacers and laminations: create controlled offsets or thicker local features.

title: Laser-Cut Assemblies & Hybrid Fabrication | Joinery, Hardware and Structural Backers
text:
Hybrid template strategy
A laser-cut face can act as a drilling or placement template for a thicker plywood backer. Clamp the template safely, locate holes accurately, transfer the pattern, then attach the precision face to the structural part. This preserves repeatability without pretending a thin sheet should carry every load.
Use joinery and French-cleat components as measured starting points and validate every interface physically.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Strong connections to TMJ2O, TCJ2O, TDJ2O, and TIJ1O through material selection, assemblies, joinery, fasteners, manufacturing planning, prototyping, and evaluation.

Next: apply these decisions to a useful Tool Holder.

title: Wall + Bench Tool Module | French Cleats and Removable Shop Organization
text: Design a visually organized holder for a related group of tools. It must mount vertically, be removable quickly as one module, and remain useful or stable when taken to a workbench.

title: Wall + Bench Tool Module | French Cleats and Removable Shop Organization
text: Design a visually organized holder for a related group of tools. It must mount vertically, be removable quickly as one module, and remain useful or stable when taken to a workbench.

title: Wall + Bench Tool Module | French Cleats and Removable Shop Organization
text:
Two operating states


On the wallVisible · organized · secure · accessible


On the benchStable · portable · usable · easy to return

title: Wall + Bench Tool Module | French Cleats and Removable Shop Organization
text:
System decisions
Consider a French cleat or other approved removable mounting interface, a thicker structural backer, 1/4 inch precision faces, dowels, pins, screws, holes, slots, combs, trays, labels, and shadow-board cues. Design a handle or safe grip only if it does not interfere with mounted use or tool retention.
The wall rail, wall attachment, load path, and structural fasteners must be selected and approved for the actual installation. A thin laser-cut plywood face is not a rated wall-mounting system.

title: Wall + Bench Tool Module | French Cleats and Removable Shop Organization
text:
Test plan

Load and remove each tool while the module is mounted.
Remove and carry the complete module using the intended grip.
Place it on the bench and use tools without holding the module.
Check tipping, sliding, sharp edges, snagged cords, and tool collisions.
Confirm the module returns to the wall without a delicate alignment routine.
Revise at least one dimension or feature from test evidence.

Explore French-cleat modules and tool-holder kits as component references.

Ontario curriculum relevance: Strongly relevant to TMJ2O, TTJ2O, TCJ2O, TDJ2O, and TIJ1O projects involving measurement, manufacturing, tool organization, material selection, assemblies, ergonomics, testing, and iteration. Electronics contexts may support TEJ2O.

title: Pill-Bottle Organizer | Five Reference Assemblies
text:
Bill-of-material and parameter routine
For any selected reference:

Measure at least three bottles: body diameter, cap diameter, height and any taper.
Choose the controlling diameter and required radial clearance.
Calculate opening = largest measured body + 2 × radial clearance.
Set centre spacing from cap diameter, hand access and remaining material, not appearance alone.
Update part dimensions and BOM before nesting.
Cut an opening coupon, record actual fit, then revise the source.
Dry-assemble; test insertion, removal, labels, tipping and collisions.

title: Pill-Bottle Organizer | Five Reference Assemblies
text:
Physical-test record
All five files currently have status unverified. Do not change that label because the SVG opens correctly. Record the material, measured thickness, machine, settings reference, date, tester, actual opening, fit result, load and revision before promoting a design to fit-tested or shop-tested.

title: Pill-Bottle Organizer | Five Reference Assemblies
text:
Reference systems worth studying
The sketches below are original Technology Commons diagrams, not copied product images. Follow each source to inspect the actual system and its licence. Borrow a principle only after checking dimensions, load, access, fabrication method and the source’s current terms.






French cleat


Principle: a continuous angled interface makes modules movable while the lower stand-off controls tilt.


Adapt: add an anti-lift or anti-slide feature where impact is possible.


Source: Wikipedia contributors · page content CC BY-SA · reference link · original schematic here is AGPL-3.0 · reference only







Gridfinity


Principle: a shared pitch lets containers move without redesigning the whole storage field.


Adapt: use a consistent centre spacing or interface datum across shop modules.


Source: Zack Freedman / Voidstar Lab and Kenneth Hodson’s rebuild · MIT · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







openGrid


Principle: a regular wall field separates the mounting interface from each accessory.


Adapt: document one interface and test light- and heavy-duty versions separately.


Source: David D / openGrid contributors · core parts CC BY · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







Pegstr


Principle: parametric holders begin with the object and the host-board standard.


Adapt: measure both; do not assume imported inch pegboard dimensions match local stock.


Source: MGX3D · CC BY-NC · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







5S shadow board


Principle: a visible home position makes missing or misplaced items obvious.


Adapt: labels and silhouettes should support return, counting and inspection, not decoration.


Source: National Highways visual-management standard · Crown publication, linked for reference; no source media reused · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only







Flexible fabrication workshop


Principle: organize around workflow, shared infrastructure and reconfigurable work zones.


Adapt: map where material arrives, work happens, parts wait and completed work leaves.


Source: Open Source Ecology contributors · open-source project; linked page terms govern reuse and no source media is copied · reference link · original schematic AGPL-3.0 · reference only









Warning



Wall mounting is not a decorative SVG problem. The wall substrate, anchor, fastener, backer, load, impact and inspection routine must be approved by the responsible instructor. A laser-cut plate is not a rated anchor.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
text:
Parametric / solid CAD
Mesh / artistic modelling




Sketches, constraints, dimensions and feature history describe design intent.
Vertices, edges and faces describe the visible surface.


Best default for holes, brackets, patterns, mating parts and predictable revision.
Excellent for organic, sculptural, character, rendering and animation work.


Primary classroom tool: Onshape.
Primary artistic tool: Blender.






Parametric CAD uses constraints, dimensions and features for predictable change; mesh modelling uses vertices, edges and faces to shape visible form.


Blender can make printable models, but it is not the default for dimension-driven mechanical or fabrication parts. Onshape is the primary fabrication-modelling tool because a student can change a dimension and inspect how the whole model updates.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
text:
Additive manufacturing
Unlike subtractive processes that remove material or forming processes that reshape it, additive manufacturing creates a part layer by layer. The model must become a printable toolpath, so model, slicer, machine, material and orientation all influence the result.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
text:
Model with intent
Begin from a measured need in Onshape. Use fully considered sketches, geometric constraints, exact dimensions and named variables where useful. Build features in a sequence another person can understand and revise.
Core operations include extrude, remove, hole, fillet/chamfer, pattern and mirror. Use each because it describes the intended geometry, not merely because it produces the visible shape once. Change one controlling dimension and confirm that related features update predictably.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
section: Keep the source; export for the next job
text:
Keep the source; export for the next job

Editable source modelSTEP when solid interchange is neededSTL or 3MF for slicingSlicer project + toolpathPrinter


STEP can transfer solid geometry between compatible CAD systems.
STL carries a triangulated surface but normally no units, colour or feature history.
3MF can carry units and richer manufacturing information; support depends on the software and printer workflow.

An exported mesh is not the editable master. Retain the Onshape document/source model and record which version produced the manufacturing file.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
text:
First modelling task
Model a small identity badge or labelled spacer with controlled width, height, hole diameter, wall thickness and edge treatment. Use constraints rather than visual guessing. Change one parameter and confirm the model updates predictably. Export STL or 3MF for slicing while retaining the editable source.

title: 3D Modelling Foundations | Onshape CAD vs Blender Mesh
text:
Model checks

Is the body watertight and intended as one part or several?
Are walls and small features plausible for the selected process?
Can critical dimensions be traced to a measurement or requirement?
Is the part oriented in CAD for clarity, even if print orientation changes later?
Is the editable source saved alongside the exported manufacturing file?

title: 3D Printed Faux Enamel Pin / Jewellery | Onshape Project
text:
Inspiration, not an answer file
Study Turn 3D Printed Faux Enamel Pins Into Unique Jewellery as a process reference. Do not reproduce the author’s finished designs. Record the source and develop original artwork. Follow your school board’s safety guidelines and the course-specific information provided by your teacher; students in Mr.� Andrade’s classes can find it in Google Classroom.



The project moves from an original sketch to an editable Onshape model, slicing and orientation, printing and finishing, then evidence-based revision.

title: 3D Printed Faux Enamel Pin / Jewellery | Onshape Project
text:
Design-to-revision process


Sketch or choose an original graphic. State the meaning and intended wearer/viewer.


Simplify it for small-scale production. Remove tiny counters, narrow islands and details that will not survive printing or finishing.


Rebuild/model it parametrically in Onshape. Use constrained sketches and intentional dimensions instead of importing a finished 3D answer.


Create raised or recessed regions. Make boundaries appropriate for the intended visual effect and finishing process.


Confirm dimensions and thicknesses. Inspect overall size, base, details, holes and any attachment interface.


Export STL or 3MF. Retain the editable Onshape source and identify the exported version.


Slice. Inspect every layer, walls, top/bottom layers, infill, travel and estimated time/material.


Decide print orientation. Compare visual face quality, layer direction, supports, adhesion and strength.


Print. Use the course-specific process provided by your teacher.


Finish and colour. Use only teacher-approved methods and allow coatings/adhesives to cure fully.


Evaluate. Check legibility, surface finish, colour boundaries, comfort, attachment and durability.


Revise the source model. Tie at least one change to measured or observed evidence.

title: 3D Printed Faux Enamel Pin / Jewellery | Onshape Project
text:
Minimum-detail and test strategy
Do not copy a universal minimum feature size. It depends on nozzle, layer height, orientation, material, slicer, finishing method and printer condition. Place several representative line widths, gaps or colour wells in a small test piece before committing to a full class batch.



The same badge printed flat or upright creates different face-quality, support, layer-direction and adhesion questions.

Critically Evaluate an AI Output | Evidence Before Confidence
text:
Evaluate against criteria
Create a small table with each criterion, the evidence available, the output’s status and the next test. A useful critique produces an action: measure the real object, ask the user, open the cited source, prototype one feature, or reject the suggestion.
Next: Find and verify the source.

title: Write a Reproducible AI Prompt and Workflow
text:
A reproducible prompt names the limited job, context, verified inputs, criteria, restrictions, requested format and uncertainty rule.

Job: critique, do not redesign. Context: desk name tag on a teacher-supplied 150 × 50 mm wood blank. Criteria: name readable at 2 m; 6 mm safe margin; original one-colour logo. Restrictions: engraving only; do not invent machine settings. Output: table of likely problems, evidence needed and one test for each. Label facts, assumptions and suggestions.

title: Write a Reproducible AI Prompt and Workflow
text:

Restrictions: engraving only; do not invent machine settings. Output: table of likely problems, evidence needed and one test for each. Label facts, assumptions and suggestions.

title: Write a Reproducible AI Prompt and Workflow
text:
Workflow record
Record the date, tool and model/version shown, exact prompt or accessible export, non-sensitive inputs, output identifier, sources opened, physical measurements, checks performed, decisions, and saved file versions. A person should be able to understand what happened without seeing a private chat.
Remove personal/confidential information before sharing. Test every submitted link in the same permission context the teacher will use.
Next: Iterate with purpose.

title: Document and Disclose AI Use | Show the Student’s Decisions
Document and Disclose AI Use | Show the Student’s Decisions
Document and Disclose AI Use | Show the Student’s Decisions
text:
Example disclosure

I used [tool/model] on [date] to generate three questions for evaluating my name-tag layout and to identify claims that needed checking. I verified the blank dimensions myself, rejected the suggested machine settings because they were not from our local procedure, and changed the spacing after a printed-size test. The logo, CAD model, fabrication decisions and final evaluation are my own work.

Follow the assignment and rubric first. Disclosure does not turn prohibited use into permitted use, and hidden AI use prevents the teacher from evaluating the student’s actual learning.
Next: complete the AI Design Audit.

title: AI Literacy & Reproducible Workflows | General Design & Fabrication
text: AI can help explore alternatives, explain unfamiliar ideas, organize evidence and critique a draft. It can also produce confident errors, invented citations, unsuitable dimensions and designs that ignore the real user, material or shop. The student, not the tool, remains responsible for the decision and the result.

title: AI Literacy & Reproducible Workflows | General Design & Fabrication
text:
A repeatable student workflow


What AI can and cannot do: assign a limited job and separate facts, assumptions and suggestions.


Critically evaluate an AI output: test relevance, accuracy, feasibility, bias, accessibility and omissions.


Find and verify the source: trace a claim to current, original and authoritative evidence.


Write a reproducible prompt and workflow: preserve criteria, context, inputs, tool/model and settings.


Iterate with purpose: change prompts because evidence revealed a problem, not just to collect versions.


Document and disclose AI use: show meaningful versions, decisions, sources, licences and the student’s own thinking.


AI Design Audit: critique a flawed fabrication answer, verify it, improve it and defend the final decisions.

title: Computer Technology / Engineering Project Ideas
text: Computer Technology and engineering applications combine electrical function with physical interfaces. Fabrication is valuable when it makes a circuit safer to test, a cable route legible, an enclosure serviceable, or a user interaction easier to evaluate.

title: Computer Technology / Engineering Project Ideas
text:
Project directions


PCB layout and soldering fixture

TEJ2O · Gauge / fixture family

Design a low-force fixture that locates a small board and selected components while students plan or inspect assembly.


Process


Measure PCB → locate keep-outs → prototype supports → fit test


Skills


2.54 mm pitch, datums, board clearance, CAD, tolerance


Difficulty / size


Intermediate · under 180 × 120 mm


Material


Laser-cut sheet or heat-resistant printed parts selected for the task


Structural


Support the board without flexing or loading components


Use boundary


Keep combustible fixtures away from hot soldering work unless material is approved


Library


PCB and cable gauges


Lesson


Tolerances & Functional Parts


Extension


Add interchangeable board locators with a documented interface




Test-lead and cable module

TEJ2O / senior TEJ · Portable work module

Organize leads and cables by function so they deploy without tangling and return to a visible inventory.


Process


Workflow study → bend-radius check → comb prototypes → carry/use test


Skills


Cable geometry, strain relief, labelling, modular interfaces


Difficulty / size


Introductory–intermediate · under 300 mm wide


Material

title: Systems Design & Fabrication Track
text:
ImportantSchool board and course safety information



This public website explains design and fabrication concepts. Machine-specific safety instruction, operating procedures, assessments, and authorization are intentionally kept outside the website. Follow your school board’s safety guidelines and the course-specific instruction provided by your teacher. Students in Mr. Andrade’s classes can find that information in Google Classroom. This page is not permission or authorization to operate equipment.

title: Systems Design & Fabrication Track
text:
Why this track
The Engineering Preparation Track develops mathematical modelling through electrical and control systems. This parallel reference develops physical design judgement through fabrication systems: understand a need, investigate precedents, communicate a proposal, select materials and processes, make and inspect parts, assemble the system, evaluate evidence, and improve the design.
The strongest Ontario course connections are TIJ/TAS, TDJ, TMJ, TCJ, TTJ, TEJ, TGJ, and THJ, but the technical knowledge is useful to anyone learning how designed objects are specified and made. Select the sections that match the problem, materials, available equipment, and required accuracy.
Every project returns to six questions:

What is the situation, who is affected, and what is actually needed?
What do existing products, users, standards, and tests teach us?
What is the simplest prototype that can sell the idea clearly and produce useful feedback?
What materials, mechanisms, fasteners, fits, and processes make the system work?
What do measurements, tests, and synthesized feedback reveal about the proposal?
Should we revise the solution, the problem statement, the stated needs, or all three?


Need + criteria Investigate Create + pitch Evaluate evidence Re-question + revise

title: Systems Design & Fabrication Track
text:
Learning goals



Learning goal
Why it matters




Use the N.I.C.E. Design Process to define a need, investigate precedents, create a minimal pitchable or viable product, pitch it, collect feedback, evaluate, and iterate.
A project should begin with a situation and evidence, not a favourite machine.


Read and create sketches, orthographic views, section views, assembly drawings, dimensions, tolerances, and revision records.
Other people must be able to interpret, make, inspect, assemble, and revise the work.


Use measurement, limits, fits, datums, and introductory GD&T to express function.
Precision is useful only when it is connected to how a part must fit and work.


Explain loads, motion, interfaces, mechanisms, maintenance, and failure modes in a machine or product.
A collection of parts becomes a system only when the relationships are understood.


Select materials, stock forms, fasteners, joining methods, and fabrication processes using stated criteria.
The same geometry can succeed or fail depending on material and process.


Plan the order of cutting, shaping, drilling, threading, joining, finishing, and inspection.
A good part made in the wrong order may be difficult to measure, assemble, or repair.


Compare manual processes with CNC, laser, additive, and other digital methods.
Automation changes setup and repeatability, but does not remove design judgement.


Inspect a part, record deviations, test the assembly, synthesize feedback, and revise the editable source.
The next version should contain what was learned from the physical result.

title: Systems Design & Fabrication Track
Systems Design & Fabrication Track
text:
Material and forming processes

7. Wood preparation and shaping
Use the jointer to establish a reference face and edge, the planer to create consistent thickness, the band saw or another suitable process for shaping, and sanding equipment for controlled surface preparation. Track grain direction, moisture and stock defects, reference faces, initial and final dimensions, squareness, thickness, tear-out, and surface quality.
The result is stable, square stock for a later component or assembly. Explain where material was removed at each operation and how the reference surfaces control later measurements.


8. Sheet-metal systems
Develop flat patterns in paper or card before committing material. Study material thickness, inside bend radius, bend angle, neutral axis, bend allowance, bend deduction, K-factor as a model, reliefs, hems, seams, tabs, beads, flanges, and the effect of operation order.
Processes may include layout, shearing or sawing, notching, punching, drilling, deburring, bending, rolling, riveting, threaded inserts, screws, tabs, and resistance spot welding. Evidence should include the flat pattern, formed dimensions, bend sequence, joint plan, and fit with mating parts.


9. Metal cutting and stock preparation
Compare a horizontal band saw, vertical band saw configured for the material, powered hacksaw, cold saw, abrasive cut-off saw, manual hacksaw, plasma process, and CNC profile-cutting process. Select a method using stock shape, alloy, section thickness, required accuracy, heat input, kerf, burr, finish, speed, quantity, and later operations.
Stock preparation includes identifying the datum end, allowing material for cleanup, controlling cut sequence, deburring, marking part identity, and verifying the blank before machining or welding.

title: Systems Design & Fabrication Track
text:
Welding processes
Welding processes are separated because their equipment, consumables, heat source, joint preparation, deposition, appearance, productivity, and suitable applications differ. For every process, record material, thickness, joint type, position, fit-up, machine settings, consumables, observations, distortion, and evaluation of the finished coupon.

10. Resistance spot welding
Resistance spot welding joins overlapping sheet by applying force and electrical resistance heating through electrodes. Study lap-joint geometry, electrode access, electrode face condition, sheet thickness, coating or surface condition, current, force, weld time, pitch, edge distance, indentation, nugget formation, and peel or destructive coupon evidence.
Use it when repeated sheet-metal lap joints and two-sided electrode access suit the design. It does not create a continuous sealed seam unless the selected process and joint are specifically designed to do so.


11. MIG / gas metal arc welding (GMAW)
GMAW continuously feeds wire through the welding gun. Study voltage, wire-feed speed, travel speed, contact-tip-to-work distance, torch angle, polarity, shielding gas, transfer mode, tack sequence, starts and stops, joint gap, bead profile, penetration evidence, spatter, undercut, porosity, overlap, burn-through, and distortion.
Compare butt, lap, tee, corner, fillet, and groove joints. Use labelled coupons to connect settings and technique to the resulting bead and joint rather than judging appearance alone.


12. Stick / shielded metal arc welding (SMAW)
SMAW uses a flux-coated consumable electrode. Study electrode classification, diameter, current range, polarity, arc length, work and travel angles, travel speed, bead placement, restarts, slag, multi-pass sequence, penetration evidence, inclusions, porosity, undercut, and distortion.
Compare how electrode choice, material thickness, joint preparation, position, and access affect the result. Keep the electrode classification and parameter record with each practice coupon.


13. TIG / gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW)
GTAW uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode and may use separate filler. Study current type and polarity, amperage control, tungsten selection and preparation, arc length, torch and filler angles, shielding gas, travel speed, filler timing, autogenous versus filler-added joints, cleanliness, heat input, bead profile, penetration evidence, oxidation, porosity, undercut, and distortion.
Compare the process where fine heat and filler control, thin material, clean appearance, or non-ferrous alloys matter. Document the relationship between joint fit-up, heat control, filler addition, and the finished coupon.

title: Systems Design & Fabrication Track
Systems Design & Fabrication Track
text:
Digital fabrication

17. CAD/CAM, CNC milling, routing, and engraving
CNC begins with the same drawing, datum, fit, workholding, and inspection discipline as manual machining. Define stock, fixtures, work coordinates, tool numbers, tool lengths, clearances, operations, stepdowns, stepovers, entry moves, tabs or holding strategy, and inspection points. Simulate the complete toolpath and preserve the editable CAD and CAM source.

CNC mill: accurate holes, pockets, slots, profiles, surfacing, engraving, and 2D/2.5D machined features.
CNC router: sheet goods, wood, plastics, fixtures, signs, furniture parts, and larger 2D/2.5D components.
CNC engraving: labels, scales, panels, serials, part identification, diagrams, and graphic surfaces.

Submit the source model, drawing, CAM setup, setup sheet, tool list, simulation evidence, machine file, first-part inspection, and revised source. Continue with CNC & Digital Machining.


18. Laser cutting, engraving, and 3D printing
Use Laser Cutting & 2D Fabrication for vector geometry, calibration, kerf, engraving, fit, assemblies, and machine-ready files. Use 3D Modelling + 3D Printing for parametric versus mesh modelling, source files, slicing, orientation, supports, tolerances, and revision.
A combined project can pair a calibrated laser-cut structure with a printed connector, spacer, jig, knob, cable guide, enclosure feature, or ergonomic interface. Justify why each process suits its part, then measure the mating interface and revise the source files.


19. Manual plasma cutting and CNC plasma concepts
Manual plasma cutting introduces torch-to-work relationship, piercing and edge starts, travel consistency, kerf, lead-in/lead-out choices, dross, heat-affected geometry, distortion, cut quality, and post-cut finishing.
CNC plasma adds CAD cleanup, closed profiles, nesting, cut order, lead geometry, consumable and kerf compensation concepts, torch height control, machine coordinates, CAM simulation, part identification, and first-part inspection. The Technology Commons CNC plasma system is still being built; this section describes the design and digital workflow without implying that the local machine is available.

text:
Capstone review gates







Gate
Review evidence




1. Situation and needs
real context, users, measurable criteria, constraints, exclusions, and assumptions


2. Investigation
precedents, standards, mechanisms, materials, processes, and questions still unresolved


3. Create and communicate
minimal pitchable or viable product, pitch, focused feedback questions, and recorded responses


4. Evaluate and re-question
synthesized feedback, comparison with needs, revised problem statement, and decision

8. Fabrication and assembly

9. Validation and revision

title: Systems Design & Fabrication Track
text:
Assessment model
Track work should reward design judgement and verified workmanship, not simply the number of machines used.








Category
Suggested weight
Evidence




Situation, needs, investigation, and alternatives
15%
N.I.C.E. brief, precedents, questions, alternatives, and selection rationale


Drawings, standards, GD&T, fits, and process planning
20%
views, dimensions, tolerances, interfaces, stock, sequence, and file control


Technical knowledge and design decisions
20%
materials, mechanisms, fasteners, processes, calculations, and trade-offs


Fabrication and workmanship
20%
suitable process selection, datums, fit, finish, assembly, and serviceability


Inspection, testing, feedback synthesis, and iteration
20%
measurements, functional evidence, user feedback, deviations, failures, and revised source


Communication
5%
organized portfolio, photographs, labels, references, pitch, and explanation



A polished object with no evidence should not receive a high result. Strong work makes the reasoning visible, records where the result differs from the drawing or need, and carries the evidence into the next version.

title: Fabrication Plate Builder
text: This browser tool makes repeatable plate geometry. It opens in inches. A millimetre toggle remains available when a machine or material specification needs it; changing the unit converts the current values instead of changing the physical size. The downloaded SVG keeps the selected physical unit. The tool does not choose safe material, machine settings, joints, mounting hardware, or a final fit.

title: Fabrication Plate Builder
text:
What the downloads contain

Cut SVG: the actual full-size plate outline and holes. Open this in Inkscape or compatible laser software. Red paths are cut geometry. Optional guides are not cut paths.
Settings JSON: a text record of every builder value. It is useful for documentation or troubleshooting, but it is not a laser-cut file and this version of the builder does not import it.
Share link: the current settings stored in the web address. Send or bookmark this when you want the builder to reopen the same design.


Diameter and radius, without the jargon

For a circle, set Outer diameter. The tool calculates its radius as half the diameter.
For a ring, set Outer diameter and Ring wall thickness. The ring’s inner opening is the outer diameter minus twice the wall thickness.
For a rounded rectangle, set Width, Height, and Corner radius. Corner radius affects only the four outside corners.
For a holder hole, either measure the object and add clearance, or choose Direct finished diameter and enter the final circle size yourself.

title: Fabrication Plate Builder
text:
What happens next


1 · BuilderSet the base, measured opening, pattern and spacing. Resolve every red validation message.


2 · InkscapeOpen the SVG at 100%, confirm the document units and dimensions, then add labels, slots or project-specific geometry.


3 · Test couponUse the calibration workflow to test the actual stock, machine and fit.


4 · OnshapeUse CAD when the design depends on 3D joints, motion, assemblies, toleranced interfaces or more than one plane.


The component palettes are idea and part libraries. This builder generates repeated plate geometry. Inkscape is the 2D finishing environment. Onshape is the better tool for assemblies and 3D relationships. These are complementary workflows, not interchangeable buttons.
Need supports for the plate? Open the Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder to generate straight, angled, triangular, cross-foot or rear-easel parts with measured slots.

title: Iteration 1: Robert Abraham and the CNC Lathe
text:
Mr. Knowles used to joke that my cohort was “Iteration 1”, the first group through the program. Many of us went on to engineering at Waterloo, U of T, and elsewhere.
This year, my own Iteration 1 has graduated and started university. I want to record some of what they accomplished, especially for anyone looking for co-op students, interns, or part-time technical help.
The important context for these stories is that this was not simply the assigned course work. These students did the regular work, did it to a high standard, and then chose problems that interested them and went much further. The best description is probably an impressive engineering side quest: the main quest was already complete.

title: Iteration 1: Robert Abraham and the CNC Lathe
text:
Robert Abraham
Introducing Robert Abraham, now studying Computer Engineering at the University of Toronto. You can find more about him and his projects at robert-abraham.com/projects.
Our school offers a Specialist High Skills Major (SHSM) in Manufacturing, and Computer Engineering is one of the elective courses students can take as part of that program. One of the goals is to connect those two worlds more deliberately: electronics, controls, programming, and Linux meeting machining, fabrication, and real manufacturing systems.
In Grade 11 Computer Engineering, Robert took the initiative to work on an old Lab-Volt CNC lathe that another high school was going to throw out. Restoring it was not an assigned project. He saw a difficult, open-ended problem and decided to take it on. Before Christmas, we were already machining our first part: a Christmas tree. Here is how it happened.



Disassembling the old Lab-Volt CNC lathe as we worked through its mechanical problems.


When we opened the electronics cabinet, the wiring was difficult to trace and did not consistently follow convention, including black being used as positive on part of the DC circuit.



Inside the CNC lathe electronics cabinet while we traced the existing system and planned the retrofit.


Robert researched a replacement controller compatible with the existing Gecko drives, and we worked through the electrical and mechanical problems. The mechanical work meant disassembling parts of the machine, cleaning them, resolving issues, and putting everything back together.
The broken controller was the only component we had to replace. Everything else was done using what we already had, open-source software, or software available free through student educational access.
We ran the machine with LinuxCNC, so part of the retrofit meant setting up and configuring our own Linux-based controller computer and operating system. LinuxCNC gave us an open-source machine-control platform without needing to buy proprietary CNC control software.



The rebuilt lathe running from our LinuxCNC controller computer.


We did not have another Mastercam licence available either. Robert learned Autodesk Inventor through educational access, generated the G-code, and kept pushing until the machine ran a program.



The finished CNC lathe after the retrofit and rebuild.


That project is a good example of what I want computer engineering to be: not just following instructions, but inheriting a broken system, researching what you do not know, and making it work. The impressive part was not that Robert completed an assignment. It was that he chose to go well beyond one.
Posted with Robert’s permission. If you are looking for an intern, co-op student, or someone for part-time technical work, consider reaching out to him.
Robert Abraham’s projects: robert-abraham.com/projects

Engineering notation uses a coefficient from 1 to less than 1000 and a power of 10 whose exponent is a multiple of 3. [1, pp. 6–8]

0.00047 = 470 × 10⁻⁶

Its powers of 10 line up with metric prefixes.

title: 2.1 Charge, Voltage & Current
text:
Voltage: potential difference
Voltage is a potential difference between two points. It is measured in volts (V). [1, pp. 33-35]
A useful relationship is:
1 V = 1 J/C
That means voltage can be understood as energy available per unit of charge.

Raised-glass analogy
Imagine choosing the floor as a reference height.

a glass on the floor is at the reference level
lifting the glass gives it more gravitational potential energy
a point above the reference can be treated as positive
a point below a chosen reference can be treated as negative

Voltage works similarly as a difference relative to a reference point. In an electronic system, that reference is often called ground.
The analogy is about potential, not about electricity literally behaving like water.






ImportantVoltage can exist without current



A battery can have a voltage across its terminals even when nothing is connected and no current is flowing. [1, p. 49]

title: 2.1 Charge, Voltage & Current
text:
Current: charge in motion
Current is represented by I and measured in amperes (A).
I = Q / t
Therefore:
1 A = 1 C/s
Current is a rate. A useful water analogy is the rate at which water is being poured, not the total amount of water in the glass. [1, pp. 35-38]

title: 2.1 Charge, Voltage & Current
text:
Why coulombs matter later
Capacitors give charge a practical meaning.
A capacitor stores separated charge and electrical energy. Its capacitance tells us how much charge can be stored at a given voltage:
C = Q / V
We will use that relationship later. For now, the important connection is:
charge + voltage -> capacitor behaviour
Modern multilayer ceramic capacitors are extremely common. Open Circuits notes that a smartphone may contain hundreds of MLCCs, many used to help stabilize power supplies. [2, p. 36]

title: 2.1 Charge, Voltage & Current
text:
Quick check

What does a coulomb measure?
What is the difference between voltage and current?
Can voltage exist when current is zero?
If 3.0 C of charge passes a point in 2.0 s, what is the current?
Why might capacitors make the idea of charge useful when looking at a motherboard?







TipImprove these notes



Add one better analogy, diagram, or real component example for charge, voltage, or current.

title: 2.3 Ohm’s Law
text:
Ohm’s law connects voltage, current, and resistance. [1, pp. 76-84]
I = V / R
Rearranged:
V = I × R
R = V / I
Where:

V is voltage in volts
I is current in amperes
R is resistance in ohms

title: 2.3 Ohm’s Law
text:
Ohm’s law connects voltage, current, and resistance. [1, pp. 76-84]
I = V / R
Rearranged:
V = I × R
R = V / I
Where:

V is voltage in volts
I is current in amperes
R is resistance in ohms

title: 2.3 Ohm’s Law
text:
What the relationship means
For a resistive load:

increasing voltage while resistance stays constant increases current
increasing resistance while voltage stays constant decreases current

We will introduce resistor components in detail when we actually start using them. For now, resistance is the idea of opposition to current.

title: 2.3 Ohm’s Law
text:
A practical computer example
Suppose a USB device is operating at:

5.00 V
0.900 A

Its equivalent resistance at that operating point is:
R = V / I
R = 5.00 V / 0.900 A
R = 5.56 Ω
Both measured values have 3 significant figures, so the final result is reported with 3 significant figures.






NoteA real USB device is not just a resistor



Digital electronics can change how much current they draw as they operate. The calculated resistance is an equivalent resistance at that operating point, not necessarily a fixed physical resistor inside the device.

title: 2.3 Ohm’s Law
section: Open and short circuits are limits of the same model
text:
Open and short circuits are limits of the same model
Ohm’s law helps explain the two failure cases from the previous lesson:

open circuit: resistance becomes extremely large, so current approaches zero
short circuit: resistance becomes very small, so current can become very large

The source and wiring always have some real resistance, so practical short-circuit current is finite.

title: 2.3 Ohm’s Law
text:
Significant figures still apply
Use the number-system rules from Unit 1:

keep full calculator precision during the calculation
for multiplication or division, round the final answer to the fewest significant figures in the inputs
round once, at the end

title: 2.3 Ohm’s Law
text:
Practice

A 12.0 V load has an effective resistance of 48.0 Ω. Find the current.
A device draws 0.250 A from a 12.0 V supply. Find its equivalent resistance.
A circuit draws 2.00 A through a 5.00 Ω load. Find the voltage.
Explain why a short circuit can create much more current than a normal load.







TipImprove these notes



Add one example from a label on a real electronic device.

title: 2. Basic Electronics
text:
This unit builds a practical model of electricity before introducing specific components in detail.
Grob’s Basic Electronics is the main technical reference for charge, potential difference, current, closed circuits, Ohm’s law, power, energy, opens, and shorts. [1, pp. 22-49, 76-99]
Open Circuits is used as a visual reference for what these ideas look like inside real electronic components and power-conversion hardware. [2]

title: 2. Basic Electronics
text:
Why this order?
The goal is to understand the quantities first:

charge tells us how much electric charge is involved
voltage tells us the potential difference between two points
current tells us how quickly charge is moving
resistance describes opposition to current
power tells us how quickly energy is transferred
energy tells us the total amount transferred over time

Specific components such as resistors, capacitors, diodes, and transistors can then be introduced when we actually use them.

title: 3.2 Switches and Floating Inputs
text:
A closed switch can connect an input to a voltage rail. An open switch disconnects that path. Without another connection, a high-impedance input floats and can respond to leakage, nearby signals, static charge, or a hand near the wire.
Arduino’s official digital-pin documentation notes that an input with nothing connected can report apparently random state changes. Read the Arduino digital-pin reference.

title: 3.2 Switches and Floating Inputs
text:
Evidence check
Predict the pin state before simulation. If a simulator displays a stable 0 or 1 for a floating input, record that as a simulator limitation rather than proof of a valid physical design.

title: 3.4 External Pull-Ups and Active-Low Logic
text:
A pull-up resistor connects the input weakly to \(V_{CC}\). A switch to ground produces a low voltage when pressed. Because the pressed state is active at logic 0, the signal is active-low.



A resistor pulls a GPIO input to VCC while a switch connects the input to ground when pressed.






Switch
Connection
Voltage
Logic
Active?




open
through \(R_{PU}\) to \(V_{CC}\)
about \(V_{CC}\)
1
inactive


pressed
to ground
about \(0\ \mathrm{V}\)
0
active




When the switch closes, the resistor prevents a direct source short. The current is approximately
\[I=\frac{V_{CC}}{R_{PU}}.\]
For \(V_{CC}=5.0\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(R_{PU}=10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\), the switch current is \(0.50\ \mathrm{mA}\).
Use an overbar, /BUTTON, or BUTTON_N to show the active-low convention. State the convention instead of relying on colour or a label alone.

title: 3.6 Circuits Culminating Project
text: Complete this project before moving to the separate microcontroller strand.

title: 3.6 Circuits Culminating Project
text:
Design brief
Create a low-voltage system with:

at least two stable switch inputs using justified pull resistors
at least two logic functions and a complete truth table
visible state indicators with correct current limiting
a transistor or driver board when the output load exceeds the logic-device rating
a defined reset or idle state
one planned fault and a safe diagnostic method

Possible systems include an access interlock model, two-button game, alarm logic, bicycle-light controller, or miniature conveyor permissive circuit.

title: 3.6 Circuits Culminating Project
text:
Evidence cycle

Predict the behaviour.
Calculate using GUESS.
Draw a proper schematic.
Simulate or verify.
Build or test where appropriate.
Compare expected and observed results.
Diagnose a fault or limitation.
Explain and reflect.

Assessment uses mathematical reasoning, schematic quality, verification evidence, safe construction, troubleshooting, design decisions, and documentation.
Download the D01 digital-input worksheet.

text: This strand finishes the circuits foundation before microcontroller programming begins. A switch input must have a defined voltage, a valid logic level, and an interface that respects the receiving device limits.

title: C01 Control-System Anatomy
text:
A control system influences a process or plant. A disturbance changes the process without being requested. In a feedback system, a sensor measures output so the controller can compare it with the setpoint.



Reference block diagrams for open loop, closed loop, PID, and CNC systems.


\[e=r-y\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(r\)
setpoint


\(y\)
measured output


\(e\)
error


\(u\)
controller output



Draw a block diagram for a thermostat, cruise control system, or motor-speed controller. Label one realistic disturbance.

title: C03 Closed-Loop Feedback
text:
Closed-loop control measures output and compares it with the setpoint. Negative feedback applies a correcting action intended to reduce the error.
\[e=r-y\]
If a thermostat setpoint is \(24.0^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and measured temperature is \(21.5^\circ\mathrm{C}\), then \(e=+2.5^\circ\mathrm{C}\). A heating controller should increase its command.

title: C03 Closed-Loop Feedback
text:
Response evidence
Plot setpoint and measured output on the same time axis. Identify only features that the data support:

rise time
overshoot
steady-state error
cycling or oscillation
disturbance recovery

Examples include thermostats, cruise control, regulated power supplies, and servo position systems.

title: C05 Proportional Control
text:
Proportional control makes the command proportional to present error.
\[u=K_Pe\]
For \(K_P=20\%/{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(e=2.0^\circ\mathrm{C}\), the command is \(40\%\) before applying output limits.
Higher proportional gain often gives a faster response and smaller steady-state error. Excessive gain can produce overshoot or oscillation.

title: C05 Proportional Control
text:
Evidence table



Gain
Rise time
Overshoot
Steady-state error
Stability




low






medium






high







Choose one gain and defend the choice using the graph rather than the gain number alone.

title: C07 Sequential Control and State Machines
text: A state machine describes the present operating state, the outputs associated with that state, and the conditions that permit a transition.

title: C07 Sequential Control and State Machines
text:
Design choices

Define the initial state.
Define every input condition once.
Include timers where time changes behaviour.
Provide reset and fault states.
Decide how stop and safety inputs affect every state.

Suitable examples include an elevator, vending machine, traffic light, game, or miniature conveyor.

title: C09 Motor and Motion Control
text:
Motion control joins logic signals with power electronics and mechanical loads.
Check supply voltage, running and stall current, driver rating, switching loss, thermal path, flyback or recirculation, direction logic, and stop behaviour.
GPIO pins do not drive motors directly. Use a transistor, MOSFET, H-bridge, or driver board rated for the load.

title: C09 Motor and Motion Control
text:
Investigation
Predict speed or position response, collect sample data, graph command and measured output, identify response features, make one design change, and show whether performance improved.

Learning goal
Treat a computer as a powered circuit and as an information-processing system.

title: CS03 Computer Power and Connections
text:
GUESS example
For a \(12.0\ \mathrm{V}\) rail carrying \(3.25\ \mathrm{A}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
P &= VI \\
  &= (12.0\ \mathrm{V})(3.25\ \mathrm{A}) \\
  &= 39.00000\ \mathrm{W} \\
  &= 39.0\ \mathrm{W}
\end{aligned}
\]
The final result has three significant figures. On the Casio fx-991ES PLUS C, enter 12.0 × 3.25 =.

title: CS03 Computer Power and Connections
text:

text:

If POST fails, remove power before checking seating and restore the documented baseline. Do not swap random parts.
Submit the compatibility table, before/after photographs, firmware and Linux verification, and revised asset record.

title: SQ01 Controlled Teardown and Reassembly
text:
Pathway: Side Quest
Prerequisites: CS02 and CS04
Previous: CS08 Benchmark challenge
Next: SQ02 Fault stations
Record the known-good baseline and photograph every side before opening. Create a fastener map and cable map. Remove only the RAM, storage, cables, fans, or drive cages approved for this station.
Explain the electrical and mechanical purpose of each connector or fastener removed. Reassemble, complete the ready-to-power gate, POST, and acceptance check.
Never open the PSU. Stop for liquid, a swollen cell, burnt areas, damaged parts, or uncertainty.
Submit the photo sequence, maps, parts-tray record, and verified return to service.

title: SQ03 Storage and Expansion Upgrades
text:
Pathway: Side Quest
Prerequisites: CS03, CS05, CS06
Previous: SQ02 Fault stations
Next: SQ04 Linux inventory
State the upgrade purpose and success measure. Research physical form factor, interface/keying, port or lane availability, power, firmware support, operating-system support, and the data plan.
After approval, protect required data, install the device without forcing it, inspect before power, verify it in firmware and Linux, and run an appropriate test.
For a device visible in firmware but absent in Linux, inspect inventory, driver support, partition/filesystem state, mount state, and logs. Do not initialize, format, or overwrite a drive without explicit approval.
Submit the compatibility table, installation record, verification, and updated asset record.

title: SQ05 Power, Efficiency, Cooling, and Thermal Behaviour
text:
Pathway: Side Quest
Prerequisites: CS03, CS06, control-system basics
Previous: SQ04 Linux inventory
Next: SQ06 Repair and reuse
Predict relative power at shutdown, standby, idle, and approved load. Use an enclosed wall meter and approved sensor tools. Record power, CPU temperature, and fan evidence at the same timed intervals.
For \(74.6\ \mathrm{W}\) over \(2.50\ \mathrm{h}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
E &= Pt \\
  &= (74.6\ \mathrm{W})(2.50\ \mathrm{h}) \\
  &= 186.50000\ \mathrm{Wh} \\
  &= 0.187\ \mathrm{kWh}
\end{aligned}
\]
Draw the feedback loop with temperature sensor, controller, fan, heat source, and measured temperature. Compare one approved setting, cleaning, or configuration change using the same workload.
No internal live probing. Keep cooling hardware installed and stop for abnormal heat, smell, sound, or fan failure.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
0. Orientation, Safety, and Design







What students learn
Why it matters




Work safely, follow a design process, and document decisions and sources.
Safe, documented work is the foundation for every build, investigation, and engineering decision.



Subsections: Safety; design process; documentation; privacy and attribution
Coming out of this section, students can: Work safely, document decisions, cite sources, and keep a usable design record.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
1. Numbers, Units, and Calculator Skills







What students learn
Why it matters




Use number systems, units, engineering notation, estimates, and a scientific calculator.
Units, scale, estimation, and calculator fluency make technical results understandable and trustworthy.



Subsections: Number systems; units; significant figures; engineering notation; calculator workflow
Coming out of this section, students can: Convert technical quantities, use engineering notation, estimate results, and present calculations clearly.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
2. Electrical Fundamentals







What students learn
Why it matters




Explain and calculate electrical quantities, power, energy, sources, and loads.
These quantities explain how electrical systems transfer energy and why components behave as they do.



Subsections: Charge; voltage; current; resistance; power and energy; AC and DC
Coming out of this section, students can: Explain and calculate voltage, current, resistance, power, energy, opens, shorts, and source behaviour.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
3. DC Circuit Analysis







What students learn
Why it matters




Analyze and verify series, parallel, and mixed direct-current circuits.
Circuit analysis turns schematics into predictions that can be checked by simulation and measurement.



Subsections: Ohm's law; series and parallel circuits; Kirchhoff's laws; dividers; troubleshooting
Coming out of this section, students can: Solve and verify series, parallel, and mixed circuits and diagnose common faults.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
4. Building, Schematics, and Measurement







What students learn
Why it matters




Build readable circuits and compare calculated, simulated, and measured results.
Readable schematics, careful construction, and correct measurement make troubleshooting possible.



Subsections: Breadboards; schematics; simulation; multimeter use; measurement uncertainty
Coming out of this section, students can: Build from a schematic, measure safely, compare predicted and measured values, and locate wiring errors.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
5. Components and Applied Circuits







What students learn
Why it matters




Select and apply common components in useful low-voltage circuits.
Component knowledge lets students select, connect, protect, and test useful electronic circuits.



Subsections: Sensors; batteries; capacitors; diodes; transistors; timers; motors and relays
Coming out of this section, students can: Design and test sensor, timing, switching, power-supply, and actuator-interface circuits.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
6. Digital Logic and Inputs







What students learn
Why it matters




Create stable digital inputs and analyze combinational and sequential logic.
Stable inputs and Boolean logic connect physical switches and sensors to dependable digital decisions.



Subsections: Logic levels; pull-ups and pull-downs; debouncing; logic gates; truth tables; state
Coming out of this section, students can: Build stable switch inputs, complete truth tables, analyze logic, and create a small digital system.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
7. Fabrication and PCBs







What students learn
Why it matters




Turn a tested prototype into a durable fabricated or manufactured result.
Fabrication turns a tested design into a durable, repeatable physical product.



Subsections: Soldering; connectors; PCB design; manufacturing files; enclosures and fabrication
Coming out of this section, students can: Prepare a manufacturable design and produce a soldered, printed, laser-cut, or machined result.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
8. Computer Systems







What students learn
Why it matters




Assemble, commission, maintain, upgrade, and troubleshoot computer hardware.
Computer hardware work connects electrical principles to real systems, maintenance, repair, and reuse.



Subsections: Components; power; assembly; startup; Linux installation; upgrades and troubleshooting
Coming out of this section, students can: Identify, assemble, commission, benchmark, troubleshoot, upgrade, and document a computer.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
9. Linux and Operating Systems







What students learn
Why it matters




Use and administer a Linux system safely from the desktop and command line.
Operating-system knowledge gives students control over files, software, permissions, and system behaviour.



Subsections: Desktop use; files and permissions; command line; software; services; backup and recovery
Coming out of this section, students can: Install and use Linux, manage files and permissions, run commands, and complete basic administration.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
10. Programming







What students learn
Why it matters




Write, test, debug, and document programs for calculations, data, and control.
Programming turns a process or calculation into a repeatable tool that can handle inputs and errors.



Subsections: Algorithms; variables; conditions; loops; functions; files; testing and debugging
Coming out of this section, students can: Write, test, debug, and document programs that calculate, model, process data, or control a task.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
11. Microcontrollers







What students learn
Why it matters




Connect code to protected sensors, inputs, outputs, communication, and actuators.
Physical computing joins code, sensors, outputs, timing, and electrical protection in one system.



Subsections: Inputs and outputs; sensors; timing; communication; actuators; state machines; data logging
Coming out of this section, students can: Create a protected sensor-and-actuator system using a microcontroller or single-board computer.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
12. Networking and Administration







What students learn
Why it matters




Explain networks and operate small classroom services using defensive practices.
Networking explains how devices communicate and how small services are operated safely.



Subsections: Addresses; protocols; diagnostics; secure remote access; services; users and backups
Coming out of this section, students can: Configure and diagnose a small network or classroom service using defensive administration practices.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
13. Data Science and Machine Learning







What students learn
Why it matters




Prepare, visualize, model, and evaluate non-personal data responsibly.
Data science helps students turn measurements into evidence while recognizing uncertainty and bias.



Subsections: Data preparation; visualization; regression; classification; model evaluation; responsible use
Coming out of this section, students can: Clean, visualize, model, and evaluate a non-personal dataset and explain the limits of the result.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
14. Language Models and Applied AI







What students learn
Why it matters




Explain, use, ground, and evaluate small language-model applications responsibly.
Understanding language models helps students use, test, and evaluate artificial intelligence responsibly.



Subsections: Tokens; prediction; small models; prompting; grounding; evaluation; responsible use
Coming out of this section, students can: Build or evaluate a small grounded artificial-intelligence application with documented tests and limits.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
15. Culminating Projects







What students learn
Why it matters




Plan, build or simulate, test, revise, and explain an integrated technology project.
A culminating project combines design, construction, programming, testing, revision, and communication.



Subsections: Requirements; design; build or simulation; testing; revision; technical communication
Coming out of this section, students can: Deliver a working or simulated technology project supported by evidence, revision, and a technical explanation.

title: TEJ Curriculum Roadmap
text:
16. Control Systems and CNC







What students learn
Why it matters




Model or build systems that use sensing, decisions, feedback, and safe states.
Control systems show how sensing, decisions, and feedback produce safe, useful machine behaviour.



Subsections: Open and closed loop control; hysteresis; proportional control; PID; interlocks; motion and CNC
Coming out of this section, students can: Model or build a feedback-controlled system with safe states, interlocks, and measured response.

title: H01 Safety and Lab Practice
text:
Safety boundary
Use protected extra-low voltage, a current-limited source, correctly rated conductors and components, and teacher approval before energizing. Never connect classroom breadboards or meters to mains voltage. Never use resistance or continuity mode on an energized circuit.
